entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Ninth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 135 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 124 · Monday, the Ninth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

135 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE NURSERY DESK: THE SENIOR CIRCUIT'S PUPILS TAKE THE FALL STARS BY SEVEN RUNS TO FOUR — CONFIDAN OF THE RED STOCKINGS' NURSERY CARRIES OFF THE MEDAL, SUSANA OPENS THE EVENING AT THREE-AND-A-HUNDRED MILES AN HOUR, AND THE DECIDING RUN COMES HOME BY A LOST ART, THE SQUEEZE

The hardest-hitting young man in the desert now owns the hardware to match. Yerlin Confidan, an outfielder in the Reds' nursery who has spent the autumn striking balls harder than anyone in the developmental circuit, doubled, drew a bases-loaded walk, and was named Most Valuable of the twentieth annual Fall Stars Game on Sunday night at Salt River Fields at Talking Stick, his National League pupils prevailing over the junior circuit's by 7-4 — the showcase, ten of the game's hundred best prospects on the card, that this paper billed only yesterday morning.2

The radar did the early talking. Jarlin Susana, the Washingtons' right-hander and the Fall League's hardest thrower, opened the game with fastballs of 102.7 and 103.1 mph and finished off Zion Rose — the Royals' outfielder taken sixth overall in the summer's draft — with an 88 mph sweeper, averaging 101.2 mph through a scoreless first inning.2 Kyle DeBarge of the North Stars was the bat of the evening, 2-for-2 with a double, a walk, two runs and two stolen bases, his 104.2 mph single the hardest-struck ball of the night; in the fifth he manufactured a run entirely alone, doubling off the Dodgers' left-hander Luke Fox and breaking for third with a jump so ambitious that the pitcher simply threw the ball away.2 Welbyn Francisca, the Cleveland infielder who leads the league's hitters at .419, added two of the finest defensive plays of the night at shortstop for good measure.2

Fox, to his credit, gathered himself after the DeBarge misadventure and struck out the side — the last of his victims, caught looking at a 93.4 mph four-seamer, being Aaron Parker of the Blue Jays, who had carried off the home-run derby's crown only the night before, as these columns recorded yesterday. The decision came in the eighth: Kevin Bazzell, a Washington catcher who had just erased a base-stealer with a throw of 1.86 seconds from mitt to bag, lined a 100.3 mph double, and Justin DeCriscio of the Mission nine brought him home by the lost art itself — a safety squeeze laid so gently on the grass before the plate that he beat it out for a single. The schoolhouse, the Herald is satisfied to report, remains in good order.2

THE LABOR DESK: 'DO NOT LOCK OUT BASEBALL' — MARTINEZ OF THE THREE CY YOUNGS, AMONG THE MOST PUNISHED MEN OF THE 1994 STOPPAGE, BIDS BOTH HOUSES FIGURE IT OUT FOR THE FANS WITH TWO-AND-TWENTY MORNINGS LEFT ON THE AGREEMENT

Pedro Martinez chose the tenth annual gala of his own foundation, at Boston on Saturday, to say what the sport's two houses have spent the autumn not saying to each other. "I feel for the fans, and I know when it's good, and it's good, baseball is good right now," the Hall of Famer said, by the account of Boston's own Herald — a paper of kindred name and, on this evidence, sound judgment in whom it quotes. "So stop the crap around and get something done and don't lock out baseball for the fans." He owned to being, honestly speaking, pissed — the word is his, and this desk prints it with the century's pardon — and he addressed the appeal to both sides of the table: "Please, for the fans, both sides, figure it out, a good way to get it done, and do not lock out baseball."3

Few men living are better credentialed to give the warning. When the strike of 1994 stopped the season, Martinez was a young arm on a Montreal club that owned the best record in baseball at 74-40 and dreams of a championship that died with the schedule — and the same cancellation left him a single day short of arbitration eligibility, so that the wage his talent had earned waited another year on the calendar's cruelty. "I was one of the most punished players at that moment because I had talent, and I needed to wait until arbitration to make my money," he said. "I might be insignificant, but I lived it before. I experienced that before."3

The calendar he addresses is not a sentimental one: the collective agreement dies on the 1st of December — 22 mornings from this one — with the owners' latest offer, tendered Tuesday last, proposing to delay their salary cap's arrival to 2028 rather than to withdraw it, and the union standing where it has stood throughout. "Back then, there was a need for other things to change, and they changed for the better," Martinez said of 1994. "This time, there's no excuse." The Herald's sympathies on matters of the purse are of long record and want no restating here; it observes only that when a man with three Cy Young trophies and a plaque at Cooperstown says the fans do not deserve to be mistreated, both houses might profitably take the afternoon to listen.3

THE LAURELS DESK: FIVE NIGHTS OF HARDWARE BEGIN WITH THE ROOKIES THIS EVENING — MESSICK'S CANDIDACY CARRIES A SIX-AND-THIRTY-YEAR CLEVELAND DROUGHT, THE WRITERS VOTE A RELIEVER'S PRIZE FOR THE FIRST TIME, AND THE HERALD REMINDS THE READER THAT POLLS ARE POLLS

The silverware season proper opens tonight. The writers' association reads its Rookie of the Year verdicts this evening at 7 o'clock Eastern on the MLB Network — the first of the week's awards, long marked on this paper's calendar. The Managers of the Year follow Tuesday; Wednesday doubles the bill, the Cy Youngs and the writers' new Reliever of the Year prizes read that night while the league stages its own MLB Awards from the Chelsea Theater at the Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas, the Hank Aaron awards, the Rivera and Hoffman reliever medals, the Comeback men and the All-MLB teams among the honors, with the comedian Roy Wood Jr. and Mookie Betts holding the gavels; and the Most Valuable verdicts close the week Thursday.4

Tonight's business first. The National League's rookie case lies among three: JJ Wetherholt of the Mound City nine, whose glove at second base banked 25 outs above average; Carson Benge, the Mets' outfielder, 20 home runs and the most balanced ledger of the trio; and Sal Stewart of the Cincinnatis, whose 112 runs driven in stood third in all the game. The American League's is a two-man argument of the everyday against the every-fifth-day: Detroit's Kevin McGonigle and his .806 on-base-plus-slugging against Cleveland's Parker Messick, who threw 186 and one-third innings to a 2.56 earned-run average — work good enough that he stands among the Cy Young finalists besides, only the sixth rookie ever to finish in that balloting's top three, after Skenes, Fernández, Gooden, Valenzuela and Fidrych. Should Messick prevail tonight, he ends the second-longest rookie drought in the game: no Cleveland man has taken the award since Sandy Alomar in 1990, a wait exceeded only by San Diego's, running since Benito Santiago in 1987.4

The week's other arguments, with the Herald's standing rule beside them. MLB.com's final staff poll of late September made Pete Crow-Armstrong its unanimous choice for the National League's Most Valuable — all 38 first-place votes — and made Misiorowski and Schlittler its unanimous choices for the two Cy Youngs; a poll is a poll, its sponsor is named, and the trophies themselves are decided by the ballot alone, which is read this week and not before. Among the managers, Pat Murphy, lately champion of the world, seeks a third Manager of the Year in succession, while opposite him stand two mid-season inheritors: Don Mattingly, under whom the Phillies played to the fourth-best record in the game after a 9-19 beginning, and Chad Tracy, who steadied the Boston club to its Wild Card berth — and who, should he win, makes the Tracys, father Jim and son Chad, the first father and son ever to take any of the writers' awards. The writers vote a reliever's prize for the first time this year besides; whether their electors and the panel of old relievers who award the Rivera and Hoffman medals can agree on the same arms Wednesday night is precisely the sort of question the Herald keeps its subscriptions for.4

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE THIRTY FRONT OFFICES REPAIR TO THE DESERT WITH NINESCORE FREE AGENTS AND MORE ON THE BOOKS — THE GENERAL MANAGERS CONVENE AT LAS VEGAS UNDER THE LOCKOUT'S SHADOW, MINDFUL THAT THE LAST SUCH NOVEMBER SIGNED AWAY NEARLY A THOUSAND MILLIONS BEFORE THE FREEZE

The winter's commerce takes a roof this week: executives of all thirty clubs gather at the Aria hotel of Las Vegas for the annual General Managers Meetings — the convening these columns flagged twice last week — with more than 180 free agents on the open market and the agents who represent them working the same corridors, a convenience the telephone winter never affords. The business sits under one long shadow. With the collective agreement expiring December 1, the trade braces for a November of unusual urgency, and the precedent is exactly five winters old: in 2021, with a lockout looming, Seager signed for ten years and $325 million, Semien for seven years and $175 million, Báez for six and $140 million, and the pitchers Scherzer, Ray and Gausman for nine figures apiece — six men and $995 million subscribed before the freeze came down, with eight more at $50 million or better in the same scramble.5

The welcome wagon carries names the Herald's readers met only this past week. Randy Flores, whose removal from St. Louis to the head of Houston's baseball operations these columns have chronicled, attends his first meetings in that chair, as does Taylor Smith, late of the Rays and the Red Sox, now atop the Athletics' operation; among the second chairs come Rob Cerfolio, promoted at St. Louis only Friday as Saturday's columns told, Cam Castro, the Athletics' new general manager out of the champions' development rooms, and Jared Banner of the Orioles, while Anirudh Kilambi of the Washingtons attends his first such meetings in the general manager's office he has held since last December.5

What the corridors will deal in is talk, and the talk has its favorite names. The Gulf Coast club will be asked all week about Drew Rasmussen, whose $20 million wage for next season would be the largest in the franchise's books — the baseball operations chief Erik Neander professes "every intention" of keeping his ace, which is what a man says in either case. Seattle's Dipoto, never bashful in the market, holds a stocked rotation and a bare cupboard of hitting, so the names of Kirby and Hancock will circulate; Abrams of the Capital nine, Marte of the Desert nine, Kwan of the Lake Erie men and Peña of the Houston nine will all be spoken of, chiefly by men who do not employ them. And the eight qualifying-offer men — Arozarena, Lowe, Suzuki, Rogers, Bauers, Morejon, Jeffers and Bednar — have until the 17th at 4 o'clock Eastern to answer their $23.15 million tenders. The industry's consensus holds that all eight decline, and history leans the same way: of the 165 men ever tendered the offer, just 18 have accepted — though the reader will note, as the agents surely do, that four of those 18 came only last winter.5

THE PANTHEON DESK: EIGHT NAMES WAIT ON SIXTEEN VOTES — THE CONTEMPORARY ERA PANEL TAKES UP BILL WHITE, FIRST BASEMAN, BROADCASTER AND PRESIDENT OF THE NATIONAL LEAGUE, WITH ITS VERDICT SET FOR THE SIXTH OF DECEMBER

The Hall of Fame's winter docket has opened its first argument. The Contemporary Baseball Era committee — the panel of 16 that weighs managers, executives and umpires — reads its results on Sunday, the 6th of December, with eight candidates on its ballot, and the columnist Anthony Castrovince spent Sunday making the case for the most varied life among the eight: Bill White, now 92, whom Cooperstown honored only last summer with the Buck O'Neil Award, a distinction seven people in all have held, for his impact on the game beyond its box scores. O'Neil himself received that honor in 2008 and his plaque in the gallery posthumously in 2022; White's partisans would prefer to see the order reversed.6

The case wants no padding, only addition. The player: thirteen seasons, a .286 average, 1,706 hits and 202 home runs, eight All-Star selections, seven consecutive Gold Gloves at first base, third in the Most Valuable balloting of 1964 and a champion that same October with the Cardinals. The broadcaster: the first Black play-by-play man ever engaged by a major-league club, hired to the Yankee air in 1971 and seated beside Phil Rizzuto for the better part of eighteen seasons, his call of Bucky Dent's home run in the playoff of 1978 among the catalogue's treasures. The executive: five years as president of the National League from 1989, the man in the chair when the league added the Marlins and the Rockies in 1993. And the road beneath it all: signed out of Hiram College by the Giants in 1953, the second Black player in the Carolina League, the desegregator of several minor-league clubs, and nearly two years in the Army besides.6

No single line of the ledger, Castrovince allows, carries Cooperstown by itself; the argument is the totality — a professional life touching parts of five decades, each room entered first or nearly first, and the door held open behind him. "Bill had no choice but to accept that job," his old teammate Bob Gibson once said of the league presidency. "Not for himself but for other people." White's own accounting was always simpler: "I demanded to be recognized for what I accomplished. Nothing more." The Herald, which keeps a standing affection for men who did several jobs well in an age that prefers one job done loudly, will have the panel's answer on the first Sunday of December.6

A Monday that opens the winter's busiest week. The writers read their first verdicts this evening — the rookies, as foretold — with the managers Tuesday, the Cy Youngs Wednesday and the Most Valuable men Thursday; the thirty front offices convene meanwhile at Las Vegas, where the league also stages its Wednesday awards theater, so that Nevada holds very nearly the whole apparatus of the game this week; and the courtroom at Brooklyn resumes its own proceedings Thursday, as Sunday's columns noted. The forward ledger, ruled open at first light as the house requires, stands unmoved: nothing on the card before the spring exhibitions of Friday, the 19th of February, 102 mornings from this one, with Opening Night 135 mornings off on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 The 17th keeps its double appointment eight mornings hence — qualifying answers and silver bats together — the Hall's Contemporary Era panel reports on the 6th of December, and the collective agreement has 22 mornings left to live, a circumstance on which the week's plainest sermon was preached Saturday at Boston, gratis, by a man with three Cy Young trophies. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Eighth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 136 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 123 · Sunday, the Eighth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

136 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE NURSERY DESK: THE UNDERSTUDY STEALS THE SHOW — PARKER OF THE TORONTO SCHOOLING, HANDED A DERBY INVITATION ON SHORT NOTICE, OUT-SLUGS THE AUTUMN FIELD WITH NINETEEN CIRCUIT CLOUTS AND CARRIES THE CROWN TO THE CATCHERS' ROOM

The Arizona Fall League's home-run derby, which these columns flagged Thursday among the week's appointments, went off Saturday night and handed its trophy to a man who was not on the original bill. Aaron Parker, a catcher of 23 in the Blue Jays' system, entered the field as a late substitute for the Dodgers' young prospect Chase Harlan, drew the seventh position of the eight, and proceeded to out-hit every invited guest: he led all entrants with 19 home runs in sum and beat the Cardinals' prospect Tai Peete in the final round by a count of 2 to 1.2

The power is no rumor newly minted. Parker struck a career-best 19 home runs this season — his first campaign of double figures as a professional, and precisely the number, the reader will smile to note, that he totaled across Saturday's rounds — and his autumn work for Mesa includes a drive measured at 451 feet.2 He joins a short and instructive roll of derby champions: the Pirates' giant Tony Blanco Jr. took last year's edition with an exhibition the desert still talks about, one ball leaving his bat at 122.9 mph.2

The main event follows directly: the Fall Stars Game, the autumn circuit's twentieth annual showcase, convenes this very evening at Salt River Fields at Talking Stick, 8 o'clock Eastern, with ten of the game's hundred best prospects on the two rosters and the Rangers' shortstop Sebastian Walcott at the head of the bill — the particulars as this paper laid them out Thursday.3 The nursery columns remind the reader why the exhibition earns its ink: last November's Fall Stars leadoff man was Kevin McGonigle, who spent this past week as a finalist for the Rookie of the Year.3

THE CHRISTENING DESK: BEFORE YOU ARE A YANKEE, YOU ARE A HIGHLANDER — THE BRONX MEN'S TOP FARM CLUB REACHES BACK TO 1903 FOR ITS NEW NAME, AND THE DEADBALL DESK PRONOUNCES IT THE WINTER'S FINEST SIGNING

A piece of news after this paper's own heart arrived Saturday from the anthracite country of Pennsylvania: the Yankees' Triple-A club, these fourteen seasons the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders, has rechristened itself the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre Highlanders — the very name the parent franchise wore from 1903, when it came north from Baltimore, through 1912, in honor of its ballpark's perch on the high ground of upper Manhattan. "Before they were the Yankees, they were the Highlanders," said the club president Sean Reilly. "And now, once again, before you're a Yankee, you're a Highlander."4 The desk that still sets its type by the standards of that era declares the sentiment unimprovable.

The announcement was made a festival: an all-day affair at PNC Field with food trucks, live music and a drone show, the proceedings carried live on the Yankees' own network with the broadcaster Michael Kay as master of ceremonies, and the Yankee grandee Tino Martinez and the sometime manager Joe Maddon — a son of nearby Hazleton — among the guests. Highlanders is the fourth identity in the franchise's books, after the Red Barons of 1989 through 2006 (a Phillies affiliate in those days), the plain Yankees of 2007 through 2012, and the RailRiders since; the coming season is the club's twentieth as the Bronx men's top farm.4

The new livery splits its loyalties agreeably between the mountains and the Bronx. The primary mark is a bear in hiking kit shouldering a bat beneath a pinstriped sky — an homage, the club allows, to a genuine bear occasionally sighted in the ballpark's parking lot — with a campfire of bat-logs among the secondary marks, all from the Louisville design house that drew the Hudson Valley Renegades' pinstriped heavens besides; the home uniforms keep pinstripes, a Yankees sleeve patch and an interlocking SWB. The mascot Champ, a bleacher creature by species, stays on. And the clerks note two fine prints: at 32 characters the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre Highlanders own the longest name in professional baseball, and the club plays in neither Scranton nor Wilkes-Barre but in the town of Moosic. The Highlanders take the field March 26 against the Worcester Red Sox, with the home opener set for April 6.4

THE FAR PACIFIC DESK: A GUARDIAN OF THE OTHER OCEAN PUTS TO SEA — TSENG OF THE FIVE-AND-TWENTY SAVES IS POSTED FROM TAIWAN, HIS WINDOW OPEN THIS VERY MORNING AND SHUT TWO DAYS BEFORE CHRISTMAS, IF THE LOCKOUT DOES NOT SHUT IT FIRST

A week to the day since Teruaki Sato weighed anchor, the autumn's eastward traffic gains another vessel. Jyun-Yue Tseng, right-handed closer of Taiwan's Fubon Guardians — no kin to the Cleveland club of that name, whose November is passing in a Brooklyn courtroom elsewhere in these columns — is entering the posting system, and the thirty clubs may treat with him from this very Sunday until December 22.5

The ledger travels well. Tseng is 25, and this season in the Chinese Professional Baseball League he went 5-3 with 25 saves across 48 games, striking out 65 men against 13 walks in 52 and one-third innings. The international stage has seen him twice: in this year's World Baseball Classic he threw hitless innings against South Korea and the Czech Republic and banked a save, his four-seam fastball averaging 93.7 mph against the Koreans with a cutter alongside. The résumé runs back further than most — he pitched in the Little League World Series of 2014, and was the CPBL's Rookie of the Year in 2021.5

The counting-house terms are the standard tariff — a signing club owes his Taiwan employers a posting fee starting at a fifth of the first 25 millions of any major-league contract — but the calendar is the clause to watch. The collective agreement dies on the 1st of December with a lockout widely expected, and the freeze may cut Tseng's negotiating window short by three weeks; the winter's every transaction now runs ahead of that same weather, as the Herald's labor columns have had steady occasion to observe.5

THE COURTROOM DESK: 'THERE WAS NO MORE INFORMATION LIKE THAT' — A COOPERATING BETTOR SAYS THE INSIDE WORD ON CLASE'S PITCHES DRIED UP WHEN THE MIZUHARA SCANDAL BROKE, AND THE WEEK'S TESTIMONY CLOSES ON THE QUESTION OF THE CHICKENS

The pitch-rigging trial of Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz, whose Thursday session these columns reported Friday, closed its week with the testimony of Luis de Aza Baez, a cooperating government witness who told the Brooklyn jury he placed dozens of bets and won thousands of dollars on the velocity of selected Clase pitches in 2023 "because I had inside information." The word came never from Clase himself, he said, but from Enoc Pena, an associate of the pitcher's, often through a group chat titled "Uber Inc." — its members, like the witness, ride-share drivers in Massachusetts at the time. De Aza Baez opened a betting account in his wife's name to raise his limits and folded the pitch wagers into parlays to fatten the payouts.6

The detail that lifts the day's testimony into the historical record is where the well ran dry. When he asked for more such information in 2024, De Aza Baez testified, he was told that because of "what was going on with Ohtani, there was no more information like that" — the season the sporting world learned that millions had moved from Shohei Ohtani's bank account to an illegal bookmaking operation, a theft of nearly 17 millions to which the interpreter Ippei Mizuhara later pleaded guilty and for which he now sits in prison, Ohtani himself cleared of all wrongdoing. One scandal's scrutiny, by this account, starved another.6

The jury was also shown a text message Clase is alleged to have sent Pena on September 30, 2023, speaking of "killing the first two chickens" — instructions, the witness said, to bet on a Clase pitch to an inning's third batter, but only if the first two had been retired; Clase did not appear in that day's game, and the defense maintains that roosters and chickens in such messages often referred to cockfighting, a legal pastime in the Dominican Republic. De Aza Baez acknowledged he will forfeit $69,000 in winnings and testify truthfully in exchange for the government dropping a wire-fraud charge against him. "This is a case about big talk and small bets," said Todd Spodek, counsel to the co-defendant Robinson Vásquez Germosen, after the session. The proceedings resume Thursday; the Herald's practice is unchanged — the allegations are reported as allegations, and the verdict is left to the jury.6

THE INFIRMARY WARD AND THE INK DESK: CARROLL OF THE SONORAN NINE HAS HIS ELBOW SWEPT CLEAN AND IS PROMISED FOR THE SPRING — THE METROPOLITANS KEEP THEIR MENDED WANDERER STOCK FOR ANOTHER YEAR, AND STITCH A SLEEVE FOR KOOSMAN

From the desert comes news of a tidying rather than a repair: Corbin Carroll underwent surgery this week to remove loose bodies from his right elbow, the Diamondbacks confirming the operation Friday, with full recovery reckoned at about eight weeks — which lands him in the new year with a month and more to spare before the first exhibitions of February 19.71 The season behind him was a catalogue of endurance: a .239 average with 22 home runs, 78 runs driven in, 33 doubles and 17 three-base hits — the most in his league — compiled around a hamate operation that cost him most of the spring and a back that nagged him through the second half. Carroll is 26, a three-time All-Star, the National League's Rookie of the Year of 2023, and the holder, since the month's turn, of the first Gold Glove of his career in right field, as these columns recorded when Rawlings read its verdicts.7

In Queens, the ink desk logs a smaller but sweeter signature: the Mets have re-signed the right-hander Robert Stock, who turns 37 this month, to a one-year contract. Stock's 2026 ran to seven starts and a relief turn — 1-3, with a 5.93 earned-run average over 30 and one-third innings — but it held one evening worth the whole ledger: on August 31 at Tampa Bay he threw five and one-third scoreless innings in a 3-2 decision, his first big-league victory since 2019. Numbness in his fingers, a souvenir of March surgery for thoracic outlet syndrome, shelved him in mid-September; the man has pitched for eight big-league organizations, in South Korea and Mexico, and for the independent Long Island Ducks, and his persistence has now out-lasted the ailment's patience.8

The same club sewed a graver stitch: the Mets announced Thursday that their 2027 uniforms will carry a memorial sleeve patch for Jerry Koosman, the left arm of the Miracle Mets, who died a week ago this morning at 83 and for whom this paper lowered its colors on Monday last.8 The patch is a small thing as cloth goes; the memory it rides on is not.

The Sabbath's ledger runs lighter than the week's and none the worse for it: a derby won by an understudy, a christening in the anthracite country that this desk will be savoring for days, a new sail on the Pacific horizon, and a courtroom gone quiet until Thursday. The forward ledger, ruled open before a word of this was set, stands exactly where Saturday left it — nothing on the card before the spring exhibitions of Friday, the 19th of February, 103 mornings distant, with Opening Night 136 mornings off on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 Nearer at hand the week fills to the brim: the Fall Stars convene at Salt River Fields this very evening;3 the writers begin reading their award verdicts on the morrow, the rookies summoned first and the Most Valuable men to follow Thursday; the general managers convene at Las Vegas in the week now opening, as these columns noted Thursday; the 17th keeps its double appointment, qualifying answers and silver bats alike, nine mornings hence; and the collective agreement has 23 mornings left to live. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Seventh of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 137 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 122 · Saturday, the Seventh of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

137 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE LEATHER DESK: RAWLINGS SETS ITS PLATINUM UPON THE TWO FINEST GLOVES IN THE LAND — CROW-ARMSTRONG OF THE SIX-AND-TWENTY OUTS SAVED TAKES THE NATIONAL HONOR, BELLINGER THE AMERICAN, AND THE BRUINS AND THE MAPLE LEAF NINE ARE CROWNED THE BEST-LEATHERED CLUBS ENTIRE

The fielding season, which handed down its score of Gold Gloves on Sunday evening as these columns recorded Monday, took its final bow Friday night: Rawlings announced its Platinum Glove winners — the best defender in each league, any position considered — and both medals went to first-time holders. The National League's platinum belongs to Pete Crow-Armstrong, the Cubs' center fielder, and the case was not close by the instruments' lights: his 26 outs above average led or shared the lead in all of baseball for a second season running, his 16 defensive runs saved stood tied for seventh among every man at every station, and his 63 outs above average since 2024 trail exactly one player in the game — a Kansas City shortstop the reader will meet again below.3

The American League's platinum goes to Cody Bellinger, whose season in the Yankee outfield piled up 21 defensive runs saved, tied for the third-most in the majors behind only Wilyer Abreu's 28 and Brice Turang's 23 — company the reader of Monday's columns will recognize as the measuring sticks of the age. Bellinger's Gold Glove this season was the second of his career and his first since the 2019 campaign that brought him the Most Valuable award with the Dodgers; he becomes only the second Yankee to hold the platinum since Rawlings struck it in 2011, after the catcher Jose Trevino in 2022.3 The ornament has a habit of finding the champions' neighborhood besides: the National League's platinum of 2024 belonged to Turang himself.2

The team honors went north and further north. The Cubs were named the National League's best defensive club for the second year running and the third time since Rawlings extended the award to whole teams in 2020, and the margin brooked no argument — 72 outs above average and 115 defensive runs saved, each figure the best in the game by a comfortable street, with Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman both carrying individual gold, as Monday's columns told. The Blue Jays took the American League's team honor for the third time, drawing even with the Cubs for the most such awards any club holds.3

THE APPOINTMENTS DESK: THE REDBIRDS FILL THEIR SECOND CHAIR FROM THEIR OWN HALLWAY BEFORE THE MARKET CAN CALL TWICE — CERFOLIO OF THE CLEVELAND SCHOOLING IS NAMED GENERAL MANAGER AT ST. LOUIS, AND THE WEEK'S FASHION FOR DEVELOPMENT MEN GAINS A THIRD SPECIMEN

St. Louis called the press to Busch Stadium on Friday afternoon and named Rob Cerfolio its next general manager, promoting him from assistant general manager of player development and performance. The president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom, who calls this stretch of the calendar "always one of the craziest times of the year," had reason to move briskly: the club lost its assistant general manager and scouting director Randy Flores to Houston's top baseball job only a week ago, an installation this paper has chronicled since, and Friday's promotion shuts the door on any further raids of the front office.4

The new man's ladder is the fashionable kind, climbed entirely through the development rooms. Cerfolio entered baseball as a Cleveland intern in 2015, rose over a decade to that organization's director of player development, and came to St. Louis in October of 2024 among the first and most instrumental hires of the Bloom regime; in the two years since, the Cardinals' farm system has vaulted up the industry's rankings, and the club credits him as an architect of the revival. "The way that he operates and what he's accomplished in the areas that he has overseen really have stood out and make this a very smooth and natural move for us today," said Bloom, who means to widen his lieutenant's scope to every corner of baseball operations: "There's just a drive and relentlessness to how he operates that I think is really important." Cerfolio, for his part, pointed to the man seated at his left: "I trust him as a person."4

The Herald remarked Thursday that two mornings running had handed a development man a top chair — Seattle's new manager Kanzler on Tuesday, the Athletics' new general manager Castro on Wednesday — and the fashion now owns a third specimen inside the week. The reasoning has not changed since these columns offered it: the world's championship was lately won by a club of modest purse that grows its own, and every front office in the game would like the recipe. The difference in St. Louis is the direction of travel — the Cardinals did not go shopping for a development man; they simply declined to let theirs be shopped.4

THE CONTRACTS DESK: WASHINGTON SIGNS ITS WALL-CLIMBING CENTER FIELDER FOR FOUR YEARS AND THREE-AND-TWENTY MILLIONS — YOUNG OF THE IMPOSSIBLE CATCHES IS SECURED THROUGH 2030, BY THE WORD OF A SOURCE, WITH AN OPTION FOR A FIFTH YEAR BESIDES

The Capital nine have moved to keep their outfield's acrobat. Jacob Young has agreed to a contract extension of four years and $23 million, with a club option of $8 million for a fifth season, by the word of a source — the club itself had confirmed nothing by press time. The deal covers Young's three remaining years of arbitration and one season that would otherwise have belonged to the open market, binding him to Washington through 2030 with the option running to 2031, and it is the second extension of the young winter under the president of baseball operations Paul Toboni, who signed the right-hander Cade Cavalli for four years and $47 million in September.5

What Washington is buying is chiefly the glove, and the glove is of the circus kind — the clubhouse calls him Spider-Man, and the tape supports the libel. A seventh-round pick out of the University of Florida in 2021, Young led all outfielders in baseball with 20 outs above average in 2024 and has banked 14 and 11 in the two seasons since; the signature exhibit came on August 23 last, when he covered 93 feet of ground at Miami, went up the wall to rob Heriberto Hernández of a home run, and threw back to the infield to double off a runner for good measure.5

The bat, long the junior partner, improved enough this season to make the arithmetic easy: Young hit .252 with 10 home runs — as many in the one year as his whole career had held before it — drove in a career-high 50 runs, and stole 18 bases in 22 tries. The club around him finished 77-85, better by 11 wins than the season before, behind an attack that ranked third in the game in runs scored; the extension fixes one more star to a young chart that already holds Abrams, Wood, Crews and Lile.5

THE LAURELS DESK: THE OLD PLAYERS HAND WITT THE HEART-AND-HUSTLE MEDAL FOR THE THIRD YEAR RUNNING — NO MAN HAD EVER WON IT THRICE SINCE THE ALUMNI STRUCK IT IN 2005, AND ONLY BIGGIO EVER KEPT HIM COMPANY AT TWO

The Major League Baseball Players Alumni Association named Bobby Witt Jr. the winner of its Heart & Hustle Award on Friday, and the Kansas City shortstop thereby stands alone in the medal's books: three wins, all in succession, where no man had taken it thrice since the alumni established the honor in 2005. The award goes each year to the active player judged to best embody the game's values, spirit and traditions — committees of former players name one man per club, and fans, alumni and active players together vote the winner from the thirty. Witt had shared the two-win shelf with the Hall of Famer Craig Biggio, honored in 2006 and 2007, and he has been Kansas City's nominee in every one of his five big-league seasons. "One of my favorite awards I've gotten," he told MLB Network. "I just try to play the game to my best ability and go out there and give 100% of what I got, each and every night."6

The season beneath the sentiment holds up under any instrument pointed at it. Witt hit .281 with 18 home runs, 33 doubles and 45 stolen bases across 143 games; his 24 outs above average led the American League and stood third in the majors; and he became the first player in the history of the game to log at least 10 home runs and 25 stolen bases in each of his first five seasons.6 The reader of this morning's leather columns has met him once already — his is the lone glovework ledger in baseball that outranks Crow-Armstrong's over the past three seasons.3

The medal joins a queue rather than ends one. Witt stands a finalist for the Most Valuable award beside Alvarez of Houston and Caminero of the Rays, as these columns recorded Tuesday, with the verdict to be read Thursday; he is a finalist besides for a third consecutive silver bat at shortstop, as yesterday's columns told; and his pursuit of a third straight Gold Glove ended only when Walls took the shortstop's leather, as Monday's columns had it.6 As for the man's own schooling, he offered the arithmetic himself: he wore No. 17 in high school for the 15 of Pedroia and the 2 of Jeter, the two men he watched to learn how the game is carried.6

THE HOUSEKEEPING COLUMNS: SEATTLE SEATS A PROFESSOR OF CATCHING BESIDE ITS NEW CAPTAIN, LOS ANGELES PARTS WITH HALF ITS HITTING FACULTY, AND CLEVELAND RECLAIMS A WANDERING SON OFF THE WAIVER WIRE

In Seattle, the new manager Jason Kanzler — whose hiring these columns recorded Wednesday — is getting a right hand: the club is in the process of making Tanner Swanson its bench coach, by the word of a source confirming an earlier report. Swanson is a native of Washington state and a Central Washington University man come home; he spent 2020 through 2026 on the Yankees' major-league staff as their director of catching, taking on the field coordinator's duties besides from 2024, and the receivers under his instruction led all of baseball in framing runs across those seasons. He takes the chair lately held by Manny Acta, one of four coaches let go at the season's end, and the minor-league hitting coordinator CJ Gillman is expected to take the lead hitting post, though the club confirms nothing yet.7

In Los Angeles the parting is the surprise of the day: the Dodgers and the hitting coach Aaron Bates could not agree on a new contract and will go their separate ways, by the word of a source — this after the baseball operations chief Andrew Friedman had said he expected the staff to stand pat for 2027. Bates spent 12 years in the organization and shared the hitting duty with Robert Van Scoyoc for the past four seasons, in every one of which the club ranked among the game's four best in runs scored; this year's edition stood fourth in runs and second in on-base-plus-slugging before the attack went quiet in October against the eventual champions. Van Scoyoc is expected back, and the club is considering hiring a second coach to sit beside him — an arrangement on which the Herald ventured a view only yesterday, concerning a certain two-headed calf at the county fair, and which it now observes the Dodgers have kept profitably these four years. The desk withdraws nothing; it merely notes the calf's yield.8

And on the shore of Lake Erie, a homecoming of the modest kind: the Guardians claimed the infielder José Tena off waivers from Washington on Friday, days after the Nationals designated him for assignment. Tena, 25, began his professional life as a Cleveland signing out of the Dominican Republic in 2017 and debuted with the club in 2023, before the trade that sent him to Washington for Lane Thomas in July of 2024. He returns with a .222 average and 7 home runs from this past season, a bat the measuring instruments say has quickened considerably year over year, and a glove that has stood at every station save catcher, first base and center field; he is out of minor-league options, which makes the claim a commitment rather than a flyer, and the 40-man roster now stands at 37.9

A Saturday of silverware and staff rooms: the fielding year took its final bow in platinum, the Redbirds bolted the front-office door Houston walked through a week ago, and the housekeeping columns ran brisk from the Sound to Lake Erie. The forward ledger, opened at first light as the house rule requires, reads as it read Friday: nothing stirs before the spring exhibitions of Friday, the 19th of February, now 104 mornings from this one, with Opening Night 137 mornings off on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 The nearer docket wants its pencil sharpened: the writers read their first verdicts Monday, the rookies called before the rest, and the Most Valuable men follow Thursday;6 the 17th remains the winter's most crowded square, the qualifying answers and the silver bats both due that day; and the collective agreement has 24 mornings left to live. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Sixth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 138 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 121 · Friday, the Sixth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

138 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE COURTROOM DESK: THE MAN WHO CAUGHT THE PITCHES IN QUESTION CALLS THEM ORDINARY SLIDERS — NAYLOR TAKES THE STAND FOR THE DEFENSE, A COOPERATING BETTOR TELLS OF 'FOR-SURE BETS,' AND THE BOOKMAKER'S OWN DETECTIVE COUNTS EIGHT-SCORE PINGS FROM THE CLOSER'S HOUSE

The second day of witness testimony in the pitch-rigging trial of Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz brought to the stand, of all people, the man who caught the pitches in question. Bo Naylor — five seasons a Guardians catcher before an August trade carried him to Milwaukee — appeared Thursday as a defense witness in federal court at New York, where the two Cleveland pitchers stand charged with conspiracy to commit wire and honest-services fraud, sports bribery and money laundering, a year on from their indictment.2 Shown the replays of pitches the government alleges were predetermined for the benefit of bettors, Naylor pronounced them common sliders off the plate. He was behind the bat for 14 of Ortiz's 16 starts in 2025, among them the June 27 game against St. Louis in which the government says the first pitch of the home third, to the Cardinals' catcher Pedro Pages, was thrown for a ball on purpose; the scouting report on the hitter, Naylor testified, called a slider low and away a "weapon." He caught besides 7 of the 18 pitches Clase is accused of rigging across 17 games from May of 2023 to May of 2025, found none of them remarkable, allowed that carrying word outside the clubhouse walls would be a "betrayal," and said he suspected no such breach by either man — indeed, that he did not know the betting houses offered wagers on single pitches until the case became public.2

The government's afternoon told the other half of the story. Edward Canario, a cooperating witness, testified that in May and June of 2023 he bet on Clase's pitches on the word of the co-defendant Luis Arismendy Paca Méndez, who was then living in Clase's house in Cleveland — wagers running upwards of $600 apiece that a given pitch would arrive slower than 94.5 mph or go for a ball or a hit batsman, placed heaviest when the word said to take Clase's first pitch of the ninth inning, whoever stood in the box. Canario paid Paca Méndez half the winnings and swallowed the losses himself; under cross-examination he allowed that his man never claimed inside information in so many words, only "for-sure bets."2 Earlier, Joel Trella, who directs the special investigations unit at the house of DraftKings, told the court his firm had counted 160 geolocation pings from betting accounts inside Clase's residence, where a government lawyer put the number of persons geolocated at 14.2

The ledger, for the reader keeping score at home: Clase is a three-time All-Star and twice his league's reliever of the year; Paca Méndez, extradited from the Dominican Republic on the 19th of October, is not a party to the present trial; and Judge Kiyo A. Matsumoto expects the proceedings to run until the 3rd of December. The Herald reports the allegations as allegations, the testimony as testimony, and reserves its verdict for the jury, which is the one panel in this story nobody has figured out how to wager on.2

THE PENSION DESK: FIVE UMPIRES OF LONG SERVICE HAUL THE LEAGUE'S RETIREMENT PLAN BEFORE THE BENCH — WEST OF THE FIVE THOUSAND GAMES SAYS HE WAS TOLD 'SUE US,' AND HAS OBLIGED

The other courtroom of the morning belongs to the arbiters. Five retired umpires — Joe West, Tom Hallion, Gerry Davis, Larry Vanover and Jerry Layne — have sued their retirement plan and its governing committee in federal court at New York, alleging their benefits were wrongly calculated and claiming additional monies under the pension law of 1974; their lawyer, Paul B. Holmes, said Thursday the sum owed the five runs in excess of $2 million.3 West, who worked a record 5,460 regular-season games between 1976 and 2021, says that when he raised the matter with the committee he was offered a modest figure and told by the league's chief employment counsel, Steven Gonzalez, "If you don't like the number, sue us." The invitation was perhaps imprudently extended. "Does Steve Gonzalez not know my history with dealing with lawsuits?" said West, who in 2021 took a $500,000 judgment for defamation off the former catcher Paul Lo Duca.3

The suit, filed the 29th of September, names the umpires' retirement plan and its committee; the umpires' union is not a party, their lawyer explaining that the organization is small and no house of pension experts. Holmes allows that some of the disputed items could be argued either way, "but in a couple of the issues it was pretty clear that they were just shorting the umpires," and says settlement talks foundered on offers that were "not very competitive." The league declines comment, citing the litigation; Judge Ronnie Abrams has set a pretrial conference for the 11th of December.3 The Herald's sympathies on matters of the purse are a matter of long record, and they extend without strain from the men who play the games to the men who called them: five officials who spent their working lives counting to four balls and three strikes now ask only that the league's arithmetic be held to the same standard.

THE LAURELS DESK: THE SILVER BAT SHORT LISTS ARE POSTED, AND AMONG THE NINE OUTFIELD NAMES STANDS A MAN OF NO HOME RUNS WHATEVER — SIMPSON OF THE .306 AVERAGE AND SIX-AND-FORTY THEFTS CHASES COMPANY WITH ROSE AND THE WIZARD

Louisville Slugger posted its Silver Slugger finalists Thursday — the honor for the best bat at each position in each league, balloted by the game's managers and coaches, who may not vote for their own men — with the winners to be read on the 17th of November, the very day the eight qualifying-offer men must answer their tenders.5 The Herald's standing rule wants no repetition by now: these are short lists, not verdicts. What wants attention is a single entry among the American League's nine outfield finalists: Chandler Simpson of the Tampa men, who this season hit no home runs at all — the only qualified hitter in the game without one — and made the list anyway, on a .306 average that stood fourth among all qualified batters behind Alvarez, Gabriel Moreno and Luis Arraez, a strikeout rate of 7.8 percent bettered by one man only, and 46 stolen bases, second-most in the game.4

Should the voters seat him, the company is select and the precedent nearly bare. Two position players have taken a silver bat in a season without a home run — Pete Rose in 1981 and Ozzie Smith in 1987 — but Rose carried 155 career home runs to the ceremony and the Wizard 13, while Simpson has never hit one in the major leagues at any date. He would be the first non-pitcher ever to win the award with no career home run whatever, joining a fraternity otherwise composed entirely of pitchers — Valenzuela, Glavine, Hershiser, Mike Hampton twice over, and lately Max Fried — and he is already better than halfway to the live-ball record for the most plate appearances in a career without a single round-tripper.4 The slap, the sprint and the silver: the deadball desk confesses a rooting interest it will not bother to conceal.

The rest of the junior circuit's lists hold steadier names. Pete Alonso, whose first Baltimore season led the league with 43 home runs and 113 runs driven in; Junior Caminero and Bobby Witt Jr., both of whom the reader met on Tuesday's Most Valuable short lists, Witt now seeking a third silver bat in succession; the rookie Kevin McGonigle at shortstop; and, among Simpson's eight outfield rivals, the ageless Mike Trout.5

THE WAGES DESK: EIGHT-AND-TWENTY MEN OF TWO YEARS' STANDING WIN THE RIGHT TO ARGUE THEIR PAY — THE SUPER TWOS ARE NAMED TO THE ARBITRATION ROLLS, A SPRING SUSPENSION COSTS ROJAS THE CUT BY TWO DAYS, AND NOBODY CAN SAY WHEN THE HEARINGS CONVENE

The arbitration rolls gained their junior class Thursday: 28 players with between two and three years of major-league service qualified as so-called Super 2s, the top 22 percent of that cohort by service time, each with at least 86 days logged this season, now entitled to argue their wages alongside the three-to-six-year men.6 The cutoff fell at 2 years, 133 days, and the last men aboard — Boston's Tyron Guerrero and Colorado's Jordan Beck — sat upon it exactly, with Milwaukee's Quinn Priester clearing by a single day. The names of note: Louis Varland, closer for the Toronto men and a finalist besides for the writers' new relief prize, as Tuesday's columns recorded; Andy Pages of the Dodgers; the left-hander Jacob Latz of the Rangers; Evan Carter, the same Texas center fielder whose mended hip this paper logged Wednesday; and Pedro Pages of the Cardinals, whose name the reader will have met already this morning in the courtroom columns, standing innocently in the batter's box of the government's exhibit.6

The hard luck of the class belongs to Philadelphia's Johan Rojas, who finished at 2 years, 131 days — two days shy of the money. He began the season under an 80-game suspension for a banned substance and ended it on the 60-day injured list after June surgery on his right elbow; the calendar did the rest. Pete Crow-Armstrong had service enough but signed his six-year, $115 million contract in March, removing himself from the exercise; and three men who would have qualified — Edouard Julien, Jared Koenig and James Outman — were dropped from 40-man rosters this week instead.6

One shadow lies over the whole ledger. The collective agreement dies on the 1st of December and a lockout is widely expected, so no man can presently say when the proposed salaries will be exchanged or the hearings sat — the rolls are posted, and the courtroom they feed has no date on its door.6

THE INSTRUCTORS' DESK: FRANCONA SUMMONS AN OLD LIEUTENANT TO MEND THE REDLEGS' ARMS — TORRES OF THE CLEVELAND SCHOOL TAKES THE CINCINNATI PITCHING CHAIR, AND THE FLUSHING MEN SEAT A SECOND HITTING COACH BESIDE THE FIRST

The appointments week — Seattle's new manager Tuesday, Sacramento's new general manager Wednesday, as these columns have recorded — descended Thursday to the coaching rooms. In Cincinnati, Terry Francona reached back to his Cleveland years and hired Joe Torres as pitching coach, the man having spent the past five seasons as the Guardians' assistant pitching coach — two of them, 2022 and 2023, on Francona's own staff — after five more in that organization's minor-league system.7 Torres, 44, was once the 10th overall pick of the 2000 draft, by the Angels, and wandered the White Sox, Dodgers, Rangers and Rockies systems before hanging up the spikes in 2013. The job wants doing: the Redlegs' staff posted a 4.83 earned-run average, third-highest in the majors, the starters at 4.97, and the club fell to 75-87 and the bottom of its division a year after playing in October. The silver in the drawer is Chase Burns, whose 15 wins stood fourth in the National League and whose 185 strikeouts ranked ninth.7

In Queens, meanwhile, the Mets have settled on a second hitting coach to sit beside the first: Johnny Washington, 42, lately the Braves' minor-league hitting coordinator, will share the duty with the incumbent Troy Snitker, by the word of a source the club has not yet confirmed.8 Washington served under the Mets' manager Andy Green once before, on Green's San Diego staffs of 2017 through 2019, and has held the lead hitting job in Anaheim besides; the lineup he inherits finished tied for 23rd in on-base-plus-slugging and tied for 20th in runs. The club has also promoted Mariano Duncan to assistant coach and brought in A.J. Ellis as its strategy coordinator, while the hunt proceeds for a farm director to replace Green himself, elevated from that post when the managing fell to him in June.8 Two coaches to one lineup is an arrangement the deadball desk regards the way it regards the two-headed calf at the county fair — with interest, and from a respectful distance — but the Herald concedes the arithmetic: a lineup tied for 23rd can hardly claim one voice was working.

The national game spent Thursday largely before the bench — its pitches weighed by a jury in one New York courtroom, its pensions reckoned for another — and the Herald observes that of all the parties lately asking the law to settle baseball questions, the only men on the docket who ever got a call right for a living are the five umpires. The schedule ledger, consulted at first light as always, reads as it read yesterday: the first ink of 2027 remains the spring exhibitions of Friday, the 19th of February, now 105 mornings from this one, with Opening Night itself 138 mornings off, on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 The nearer docket thickens agreeably: the writers begin reading their award verdicts Monday, the rookies called first; the 17th has become a double appointment, the eight qualifying men to answer their tenders and Louisville Slugger to read its silver-bat winners the same day;5 and the collective agreement has 25 mornings left to live — the arbitration clerks, the reader will note above, are already penciling their calendar in the subjunctive.6 Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Fifth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 139 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 120 · Thursday, the Fifth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

139 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE APPOINTMENTS DESK: PUJOLS COMES TO HOUSTON'S DOOR TO ASK FOR THE MANAGER'S CHAIR — ENSBERG AND URUETA JOIN THE QUEUE, AND THE NEW MAN FLORES FINDS HIS OWN ADDRESS BOOK AT THE HEAD OF IT

The Houston vacancy draws its grandest caller yet: Albert Pujols, 46, arrived in town late Wednesday and is scheduled to interview for the manager's chair at Daikin Park this Thursday, by the word of sources the club declines to confirm.2 The playing credentials occupy their own wing of the museum — twenty-two seasons, 703 home runs, 686 doubles, 2,218 runs driven in, eleven All-Star summons, three Most Valuable Player awards and two world's championships — and the interviewers may be asked to forgive the detail that no man has hit more home runs against the Astros than their caller, among them a three-run, go-ahead blow in the ninth inning of Game 5 of the 2005 Championship Series at Houston. What he has never done is manage a big-league game; what he has done is manage winners elsewhere, piloting Leones del Escogido to the 2024-25 Dominican winter crown and the Dominican national side to a third-place finish at this year's World Baseball Classic.2 He interviewed with the Angels and the Padres a winter ago and watched those chairs go to Kurt Suzuki and Craig Stammen; he remains under contract with the Angels even now.

Behind him the queue forms. Morgan Ensberg, 51, who spent seven of his eight playing seasons in Houston silks and gave the 2005 pennant club a .283, .388 and .557 season with 36 home runs — fourth in the Most Valuable voting — is expected to interview this week, and unlike Pujols he carries a managing ledger: seven seasons across Double-A Montgomery and Triple-A Durham with four postseason berths, plus turns in the Arizona Fall League and Venezuelan winter ball. Luis Urueta, bench coach of the Rangers, will be interviewed besides, by the report of MLB Network's Jon Morosi.2

The reader who has followed these columns will remark the pattern. The man conducting the hunt is Randy Flores, the franchise's 15th general manager, introduced at Daikin Park only Monday as this paper reported — and his candidates read like his own address book: Pujols was his Cardinals teammate from 2004 through 2008, and Ensberg his teammate at Southern California in the middle nineties. Flores has said he is "looking to find someone that I can trust and can communicate with," and he appears to be taking the sentence literally.2 Brad Ausmus, whose candidacy this paper logged Monday, remains in the frame, the manager's post having been discussed when he interviewed for the general manager's job that went to Flores. The calendar presses: Flores packs for the general managers' meetings at Las Vegas next week, and the club would plainly prefer to pack a skipper alongside.2

THE HIRING HALL: THE WHITE ELEPHANTS RAID THE CHAMPIONS' SHOP FOR A GENERAL MANAGER — CASTRO OF THE MILWAUKEE PITCHING WORKS, ONCE A THROWING TRAINER, TAKES THE SECOND CHAIR IN SACRAMENTO

The Athletics on Wednesday named Cam Castro their general manager, and the pedigree tells where the game's envy points: Castro, 36, arrives from Milwaukee, where he spent the past two seasons as senior vice president of player development and performance — which is to say the Elephants have gone shopping in the world champions' shop.3 He will serve as the right hand of Taylor Smith, himself installed as president of baseball operations just over two weeks ago. The ladder behind him is pitching from bottom rung to top: a throwing trainer at Driveline Baseball in 2016, a Brewers minor-league pitching coach by 2019, then the organization's pitching coordinator and director of pitching development, and from 2022 its vice president of player development, a member of Matt Arnold's inner circle. "One of the best development minds in the game," Smith called him.3

The Herald notes the week's fashion with approval: that makes two mornings running that a development man has been handed a top chair, Seattle having given its manager's office to the Cubs' farm director Jason Kanzler only yesterday, as these columns recorded. The fashion is no mystery — the champions contested and won a World's Series on one of the game's thinner purses, as yesterday's labor columns had occasion to note, and every club would like the recipe. Castro inherits a task of size: the Athletics finished 64-98, want for pitching above all else, and play one final season at Sutter Health Park in West Sacramento before the Las Vegas ballpark is expected to open its gates for the 2028 season.3

THE RUMOR DESK: BALTIMORE HANGS A PRICE ON EVERY MAN SAVE ALONSO — HENDERSON OF FIVE-AND-TWENTY MAY BE HAD FOR A RANSOM, ARIZONA SETS MARTE BACK UPON THE TABLE, AND PASSAN CROWNS RASMUSSEN THE WINTER'S LIKELIEST MOVER

From Baltimore comes the winter's boldest storefront. The Orioles, by the report of Andy Kostka of the Baltimore Banner, will entertain trade offers on every player on the roster save Pete Alonso, as they hunt upgrades for the rotation and the outfield.4 Alonso, the reader will recall from Tuesday's columns, was the five-year, $155 million signing of last December. Every player includes the shortstop Gunnar Henderson, 25, though the asking price there is understood to be of the sort that ends conversations rather than opens them; his play has receded from its Most-Valuable-caliber heights of 2024, and the Birds would evidently sooner be overpaid than persuaded.4

Arizona, meanwhile, has put Ketel Marte back upon the table, by the account of MLB.com's Steve Gilbert, the Snakes having missed the playoffs narrowly in each of the past three seasons. The table has a peculiar geometry: Marte is signed through 2030 with a player option for 2031, and as a ten-and-five man he carries a full no-trade clause — the club may shop him, and he may decline to be sold. The sides moved past an August unpleasantness, an unexcused absence from a game at Fenway Park, but the listing itself tells the reader which way the front office leans.4

And in St. Petersburg the other shoe hovers audibly. ESPN's Jeff Passan ranks Drew Rasmussen, 31, the likeliest trade candidate in the game this winter — one season from free agency at $20 million, the richest single-year average in the franchise's books — this set against the vow of the president Erik Neander, printed in these columns only yesterday, that the club has "every intention" of Rasmussen anchoring the 2027 rotation.4 The Herald wrote then that it records the intention and will watch the deed; the deed, it develops, has already acquired bookmakers.

THE FAR PACIFIC DESK: THE MEASURING INSTRUMENTS RENDER THEIR VERDICT ON SATO — A BAT AMONG THE GAME'S SWIFTEST, AN APPETITE THAT CHASES NEARLY EVERYTHING, AND ONE SUITOR ALREADY SAID TO COOL

Since Teruaki Sato weighed anchor Sunday — the posting this paper recorded Monday, with all thirty clubs free to treat with him — the trade has busied itself with the question of what, precisely, is crossing the water. MLB.com's David Adler has now published the measuring instruments' answer, drawn from Japan's licensed tracking data, and the figures read like a strongman's calling card: an average exit velocity of 93.3 mph, which would stand roughly among the ten best in the majors and in line with Shohei Ohtani's 2026 mark; a top strike of 117.0 mph, a reading only a handful of big-league men produce in a season; a bat swung at 74.6 mph, inside the game's top 50 and nearly identical to Munetaka Murakami's; a hard-hit rate of 55.3 percent; and a barrel rate of 18.4 percent that would trail only Murakami's own.5 For the eye that prefers a single exhibit, there is an August drive measured at 480 feet.5

The asterisk is appetite. Sato swung at 53 percent of the pitches he saw last season and chased better than a third of those outside the zone; the Japanese baseball authority Yuri Karasawa reckons him a freer swinger than nearly any notable NPB hitter of the past five years. His countryman Murakami — who struck out and walked in heaps and still hit 35 home runs as a White Sox rookie this season, the most ever by a Japanese hitter in his debut year — represents the opposite church: monkish selectivity, violence only upon the chosen pitch. Sato strikes out less, walks less, and makes more contact, particularly against the breaking and off-speed stuff; Adler calls the chasing "playing with fire" against major-league pitching, and the projections split the difference, reckoning him at .247 with 31 home runs and a bat some 12 percent better than the league average in his first campaign.5

The market, meanwhile, moved a square. The Mets — one of the four clubs the insider Heyman linked to the man at his posting, as this paper noted Monday — are now said by The Athletic to be less inclined to pursue him, their winter fixed instead upon starting pitching, with Tarik Skubal the declared object of desire; Bo Bichette's decision to exercise his $42 million player option for 2027 has helped settle the club's plans besides.4 The queue for Skubal thus lengthens precisely as foretold — the Cubs' ardor was Tuesday's news in these columns — and the first lot of the fair looks dearer by the morning.

THE NURSERY DESK: THE AUTUMN CIRCUIT NAMES ITS FALL STARS FOR SUNDAY EVENING — TEN OF THE TOP HUNDRED BOUND FOR SALT RIVER FIELDS, WALCOTT OF THE TEXAS SYSTEM AT THEIR HEAD

The Arizona Fall League named its Fall Stars on Wednesday, and the twentieth annual showcase convenes Sunday evening at Salt River Fields at Talking Stick, 8 o'clock Eastern, with the MLB Network carrying the pictures.6 Ten of the game's hundred best prospects dot the rosters, six of them on the American League side: the Rangers' shortstop Sebastian Walcott, ranked No. 8 in the game and the bill's headliner, joined by the Angels' Arjun Nimmala, the Rays' catcher Nathan Flewelling, the Royals' Angeibel Gomez, the Yankees' Dax Kilby and the Orioles' Ike Irish. The National League counters with the Braves' Tate Southisene, the Phillies' Aidan Miller, the Nationals' right-hander Jarlin Susana and the D-backs' Demetrio Crisantes. Two more of the hundred — Detroit's Zyhir Hope and the White Sox's Caleb Bonemer — were named to the honor but will not play, their Fall League terms already ended; and the Guardians' Welbyn Francisca, who leads the circuit at .409, supplies the local menace. The autumn league's home-run derby precedes the whole affair on Saturday.6

Why the exhibition merits the Herald's ink, the week's own columns attest: a year ago Kevin McGonigle led off the Fall Stars Game for the American side, and this week the writers named him a finalist for the Rookie of the Year, as this paper recorded Tuesday. The autumn circuit is where next November's short lists take their batting practice.6

A morning of chairs, this one: a grandee of 703 home runs asks for Houston's, a champion's apprentice takes Sacramento's, and the rumor columns hang a price on half of Baltimore. The schedule ledger, consulted at dawn as it is every dawn, holds steady: the first ink of 2027 remains the spring exhibitions of Friday, the 19th of February, now 106 mornings from this one, with Opening Night itself 139 mornings off, on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 The nearer docket wants no padding — the writers begin reading their award verdicts Monday, the rookies first; the eight qualifying men have until the 17th to answer their tenders; the general managers convene at Las Vegas in the week ahead;2 and the collective agreement has 26 mornings left to live, the Herald's sympathies filed where they have always been filed. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
