entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Fourth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 140 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 119 · Wednesday, the Fourth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

140 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE LABOR DESK: THE OWNERS MOVE THE CAP'S BIRTHDAY TO 2028 AND SWEETEN EVERY FIGURE — FREEDOM AFTER FIVE YEARS FOR MEN OF THIRTY, A MINIMUM WAGE OF A ROUND MILLION, THE QUALIFYING TARIFF MARKED FOR ABOLITION, AND BOTH PENNANT WINNERS FOUND BENEATH THE PROPOSED FLOOR

The owners returned to the bargaining table Tuesday with their salary cap wearing new figures and a later birthday. The league's latest proposal to the players' union would have the cap-and-floor system begin not in 2027 but in 2028, the second year of a new agreement, with the floor set at $180.2 million and the cap at $258.2 million — roughly $9 million and $13 million higher, respectively, than the figures first proposed for 2027.2 The league's stated reason for the delay is the market now open for business: some clubs already carry 2027 commitments near or above the proposed ceiling, while others would need to raise their payrolls dramatically to clear the proposed floor, and the league says a year's grace avoids disrupting the winter underway. "The projected salary cap and floor for 2028 continues to provide more money for Major League players while leveling the playing field," the league's spokesman Glen Caplin said, "so that every fan believes their team has a fair chance to win it all."2

The sweeteners attached would arrive in 2027 regardless. The league says it will accept the union's May proposal to cut the reserve period to five years for players who have reached 30 — the first reduction below six years since the system was fixed in 1976, and one that would have freed 48 percent of this past season's five-year men a winter early. It would accept the union's proposal to abolish the qualifying-offer system entire — the very tariff under which eight men were tendered $23.15 million apiece only Monday, as these columns recorded. The minimum salary would climb to $1 million for men with two years' service, the largest single increase in the wage's history, with the pre-arbitration bonus pool fattened from $50 million to $65 million besides; and come 2028 the whole enterprise would turn to an even split of baseball revenue between the clubs and the players, with media monies centralized.2

Now the weighing, which this paper performs with its sympathies long on record. By the league's own arithmetic, twelve clubs finished 2026 below the proposed floor and would be obliged to add a combined $636 million in payroll, while eight stand above the cap and would shed $528 million. The reader is invited to run a finger down the list of the twelve — Marlins, Guardians, Cardinals, Rays, Nationals, White Sox, Twins, Rockies, Pirates, Athletics, Reds and Brewers — and to pause at two of them, the Rays and the Brewers: the clubs that contested the World's Series one week ago both stand beneath the wage line the proposal declares the minimum of respectability.2 A plan sold as giving every fan a fair chance to win it all must reckon with the fact that the fair chance just played five games in late October on two purses the plan itself calls too thin. The union's answer had not reached the wires by press time; the present agreement dies on the first of December, 27 days from this morning, and the Herald will keep the ledger open and the handkerchief in its drawer.

THE APPOINTMENTS DESK: SEATTLE HANDS THE HELM TO A MAN OF SIX-AND-THIRTY WHO NEVER MANAGED A GAME AT ANY STATION — KANZLER OF THE CUBS' NURSERY BEATS OUT ESPADA AND BECOMES THE GAME'S SECOND-YOUNGEST SKIPPER

The Puget Sound men have their new captain, and the choice runs clear outside the box: Jason Kanzler, 36 years old, lately three seasons the director of the Cubs' player development, was announced Tuesday morning as the 22nd manager in the franchise's history — a first-time skipper not merely in the big leagues but at any level of organized play.3 He becomes the second-youngest manager in the game, behind only Washington's Blake Butera, who is 34, and the third man to hold the chair under the president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto, now entering his twelfth season. He succeeds Dan Wilson, whose tenure ended immediately after Game 162 of a season the club counts among its most disappointing. "Our goal in this process was finding a manager with the ability to challenge all of us to improve," Dipoto said. "Jason has the mindset, expertise, communication skills and intensity to help create a championship standard here in Seattle."3

The resume is short on gray hair and long on ascent. A 20th-round draft pick of the Twins in 2013 whose playing days topped out at High-A, Kanzler climbed through the Houston organization across five seasons — hitting coach in the low minors, then minor-league hitting coordinator, then two years on the big-league staff in 2022 and 2023, the first of them ending with the Commissioner's Trophy under Dusty Baker — before the Cubs handed him their farm system.3 The final round came down to two men, and the reader will savor the other name: Joe Espada, the Houston manager whose vacated chair the Astros are even now hunting to fill, as this paper reported Monday. Espada and Kanzler were colleagues on those Houston staffs; the pupil, by the industry's reckoning, has taken the chair first. "This team has an immense amount of talent in all facets of the game," the new man said, "and my coaching staff and I are excited to access and unlock this team's full potential."3

THE BALLOT BOX DESK: TEIXEIRA OF THE 409 CIRCUIT CLOUTS IS ELECTED TO CONGRESS FROM THE ONE-AND-TWENTIETH DISTRICT OF TEXAS — THE SWITCH-HITTER TRADES FIRST BASE FOR THE HOUSE FLOOR, DOWN THE OLD PATH BUNNING BLAZED

The Republic gave its Tuesday to the ballot box, and among the returns came a baseball name of the first magnitude: Mark Teixeira, Republican of Texas, has won election to the United States House of Representatives from that state's 21st Congressional District.4 The ledger he carries to Washington wants no padding. Across fourteen seasons from 2003 through 2016 the switch-hitting first baseman batted .268 with 409 home runs and 1,298 runs driven in, made three All-Star teams, won five Gold Gloves and three Silver Sluggers, and collected a world's championship with the 2009 Yankees.5 There is a neat symmetry in the geography: it was Texas that drafted him fifth overall in 2001 out of Georgia Tech and Texas where he broke into the league in 2003, and it is Texas that now returns him to public life.5

The Capitol has seated ballplayers before, and the path is honorably worn. Jim Bunning threw a perfect game in 1964, pitched his way to Cooperstown, and sat in both chambers of Congress for Kentucky — the House first, then two terms in the Senate. Teixeira arrives by the same door, though the Herald notes the positional novelty: the pitchers have historically handled the nation's business, and it is not every Congress that gains a first baseman, a position whose whole trade is receiving what others throw and keeping a foot on the bag while doing it. The gentleman from the 21st District may find the skills transfer directly.

THE EXCHANGES DESK: THE WINTER'S FIRST TRADE SENDS A SOUTHPAW OF SIX FEET SEVEN TO THE MOUND CITY — THE PINSTRIPES TENDER BEDNAR BUT LET CHISHOLM WALK UNTAXED, AND TAMPA BAY SWEARS ITS ACE IS NOT FOR SALE

The winter's first trade is on the books, and St. Louis made it. The Cardinals announced Tuesday the acquisition of the left-hander Eduardo Rivera from Boston in exchange for the minor-league right-hander Juan Carlos García.6 Rivera is a specimen worth the squint: 23 years old, 6 feet 7 inches of San Juan, Puerto Rico, who opened his big-league career this April with 7 scoreless innings across his first two appearances and proved very nearly unhittable to his own kind — left-handed batters managed one hit in 15 tries against him in the majors, and across 355 left-handed batters faced in his entire minor-league career he has never allowed a home run. His 2026 in the minors read 7-2 with a 2.59 earned-run average and 71 strikeouts in 55 2/3 innings between Portland and Worcester, and he entered the season ranked the No. 18 prospect in the Boston system. García, the price, is an 18-year-old from Montemorelos, Mexico, with two seasons of Dominican Summer League work behind him.6

In the Bronx, the other half of Monday's qualifying-offer ruling emerged. The Pinstripes tendered their closer David Bednar the $23.15 million — his 35 saves this season tied for third in the league, and his ledger since arriving from Pittsburgh in July of 2025 reads 45 saves at a 2.39 earned-run average — but they extended no such offer to the second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., who therefore walks to the open market with no draft-pick tariff hung about his neck, a considerable sweetening of his candidacy.7 Bednar has until the 17th to answer; he was one of six Yankee relievers to reach free agency at once, and the club's bullpen, second in the majors at a 3.13 earned-run average, is suddenly a thing to be rebuilt.7

And in St. Petersburg, the question this paper opened Sunday — pay the ace or trade him — received the front office's answer, for whatever a November answer is worth. "Every intention right now is thinking about Ras anchoring our rotation," the president of baseball operations Erik Neander said Tuesday of Drew Rasmussen, whose $20 million option the club exercised Saturday. "We want to have Ras back. It's hard to think that we'll be closer if Ras isn't a part of this team."8 The reader with a long memory will note, as the beat men did, that Neander spoke in nearly the same register about Tyler Glasnow three years ago and traded him to Los Angeles two months later; the Herald records the intention and will watch the deed.8

THE INFIRMARY WARD: CARTER OF THE ARLINGTON MEN GOES UNDER THE SURGEON'S HAND AT FOUR-AND-TWENTY — A HIP REPAIRED, AND THE FIRST BELL OF 2027 LIKELY TO RING WITHOUT HIM

From Texas comes word that the center fielder Evan Carter underwent surgery last week to repair the labrum of his right hip, addressing an impingement besides, and is unlikely to be ready when the 2027 season opens.9 The news lands hard on a career that began at altitude: Carter debuted at 21 in September of 2023 and won a World's Series ring in his first autumn, but the seasons since have been a wrestle, and his 2026 read .194 with 9 home runs and 17 stolen bases across 391 at-bats.10 He is 24 — young enough that a mended hip may yet return the player of that first October — and the Rangers' outfield plans for the spring must now be drawn without him. The Herald wishes the young man a clean knitting and a patient calendar.

Election Day gave the paper its strangest crossover since the champions played Rockefeller Center: a first baseman bound for Congress, and the box score of the thing certified by the returns rather than the official scorer. The schedule ledger was consulted this morning all the same, as it is every morning, and the entry stands unchanged from Tuesday's dispatch: the first ink of 2027 remains the spring exhibitions of Friday, the 19th of February, now 107 mornings off, with Opening Night itself 140 mornings distant on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 Nearer at hand the docket thickens: the writers begin reading their award verdicts Monday, the rookies called first,11 the eight qualifying men have until the 17th to answer their tenders7 — a species of paperwork that may prove the last of its kind, if Tuesday's proposal at the bargaining table has its way2 — and the owners and the union now bargain with 27 mornings left on the agreement's life. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Third of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 141 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 118 · Tuesday, the Third of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

141 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE LAURELS DESK: THE WRITERS POST THEIR SHORT LISTS, THREE MEN TO A RACE IN TEN RACES — THE CREAM CITY NINE LAND FOUR FINALISTS, OHTANI STANDS FOR A FOURTH CROWN IN SUCCESSION, AND THE FIREMEN GET A PRIZE OF THEIR OWN AT LAST

The Baseball Writers' Association posted its finalists Monday evening — three names to a race, ten races across the two leagues, read out live on the MLB Network — and the verdicts follow in the week of November 9: the rookies first on the 9th, the managers on the 10th, the pitchers and the relief men on the 11th, and the Most Valuable Players on the 12th.2 The relief honor is brand new this year, the writers having at last hung a prize for the firemen, and the Herald's standing rule bears repeating before the speculating begins: these are short lists, not verdicts, and no trophy changes hands until the ballot says so. The widest grins this morning belong to Milwaukee, which placed a man in four of the five races — Jacob Misiorowski for the Cy Young, Pat Murphy for Manager of the Year, Trevor Megill for the relief prize, and Brice Turang, who adds a Most Valuable Player candidacy to the Gold Glove this paper recorded only yesterday.2

The valuable-player races first. In the junior circuit stand Yordan Alvarez of Houston, who led every qualified hitter in the game at .316, .432 and .601 with 42 home runs and 106 runs driven in, and chased the first Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2012 before falling just short; Junior Caminero of Tampa Bay, 23 years old and present for all 162 games with 42 homers of his own; and Bobby Witt Jr. of Kansas City, a finalist on the strength of his glove and a fourth consecutive year among the balloting's top seven. In the elder league the favorite is Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs, the seventh man ever to post a 40-40 season — 45 home runs, 41 stolen bases — atop the best center-field defense in the game by every modern measure. Against him: Shohei Ohtani, who has taken the award three years running and four times in all — only Barry Bonds, with seven, holds more — a finalist again despite injuries of knee and biceps that halved his pitching year, though the half he gave read 1.79 by earned-run average; and Turang, a first-time finalist at .268 with 21 home runs and 100 runs driven in.2

The pitching short lists hold their own drama. Cam Schlittler of the Yankees led his league at 1.95 and drew comparisons in the Bronx to Guidry's 1978; Dylan Cease posted a 2.40 figure in his first Toronto season; and Parker Messick of Cleveland, a rookie of 186 1/3 innings — the heaviest rookie workload since 2019 — stands a finalist for the Cy Young and the Rookie of the Year alike. The National League's race pits Misiorowski, whose 252 strikeouts led all baseball and whose 1.80 earned-run average is the lowest in his franchise's books, with opponents batting a record-low .157 against him, against the ageless Chris Sale, a finalist for the ninth time, and Philadelphia's Cristopher Sánchez, a finalist for the second straight year. Among the managers, Kevin Cash, Chad Tracy and Will Venable will contest the junior circuit's honor, while Murphy — who would become the first man since the award's creation in 1983 to win it three years running — faces Don Mattingly and Walt Weiss. The rookie lists: Kevin McGonigle, Messick and Payton Tolle in the one league; Carson Benge, Sal Stewart — whose 112 runs driven in ranked third in all the game — and JJ Wetherholt in the other. And the inaugural relief ballots: Bryan Baker and Cade Smith, who tied atop the majors at 41 saves apiece, with Louis Varland in the junior circuit; Jhoan Duran, Megill and Mason Miller in the senior.2

THE BAZAAR DESK: EIGHT MEN ARE TENDERED THE QUALIFYING WAGE OF THREE-AND-TWENTY MILLIONS — MOREJON AMONG THEM AS PROMISED, SAN DIEGO BREAKING THE CLOSERS' MONOPOLY, AND EVERY ANSWER DUE BY THE SEVENTEENTH

The qualifying wage this winter is fixed at $23.15 million for a single season's service, and before Monday's deadline eight men were tendered it: Randy Arozarena of Seattle, owner of six consecutive 20-20 seasons and a career-best batting year in his walk season; Brandon Lowe, whose 35 home runs and 96 runs driven in repaid Pittsburgh's trade for him in full; Seiya Suzuki of the Cubs; the left-hander Trevor Rogers of Baltimore; Jake Bauers of Milwaukee; Adrian Morejon of San Diego; the catcher Ryan Jeffers of Minnesota; and David Bednar, who saved 35 games in 39 chances for the Yankees.3 Each has until 4 o'clock Eastern on the 17th of November to accept the year at that wage or decline it and carry a draft-pick tariff into the open market. The historical odds favor declining: of all the men so tendered since the system began in 2012, just 18 have accepted.3

Two entries deserve the longer look. San Diego's answer on Morejon, which this paper left pending at press time yesterday, came in the affirmative — and broke a precedent in the doing, for every reliever tendered the offer before him was a closer, and Morejon is a setup man by trade, albeit one with a 2.58 earned-run average across the past three seasons entire.3 And in Milwaukee the offer went to Bauers, the Championship Series' most valuable man, whose .266, .389 and .484 with 26 home runs amounted to a career year earned on a wage of $2.7 million — the offer would multiply his pay better than eightfold. Should he decline and sign elsewhere for $50 million or more, the champions collect a compensation pick near the first round's end, the same arrangement that turned Willy Adames's departure into the 32nd pick of last summer's draft.5

THE PANTHEON DESK: EIGHT NAMES GO BEFORE THE SIXTEEN FOR COOPERSTOWN'S WINTER BALLOT — BOCHY OF THE FOUR TITLES, BAKER OF THE TWO-THOUSAND WINS, PINIELLA TWICE DENIED BY A SINGLE VOTE, AND THE LATE TED TURNER BESIDES

The Hall of Fame on Monday unveiled its Contemporary Baseball Era ballot for managers, executives and umpires: eight candidates, to be weighed by a 16-member panel of Hall of Famers, executives, writers and historians, with 75 percent of the vote — twelve hands — required for election. The results come down Sunday, the 6th of December, and any man elected joins the Class of 2027.4 Four skippers lead the bill. Bruce Bochy, with four World Series titles and 2,252 wins, sixth on the all-time ledger, is newly eligible after retiring a second time a year ago. Dusty Baker, eighth all-time at 2,183 wins, remains the only manager ever to lead five different clubs into the postseason. Joe Maddon is the man who ended the Cubs' 108-year wait in 2016. And Lou Piniella returns to a ballot that has twice — in 2018 and 2023 — left him exactly one vote shy of the doors.4

The office men round out the eight. Sandy Alderson built the Oakland club that won three straight pennants from 1988 through 1990; Brian Sabean's long San Francisco stewardship produced three championships in five years. Ted Turner, the broadcasting titan who owned the Atlanta club from 1976 to 1996 and bankrolled its transformation from cellar fixture to the team of the nineties, stands for election posthumously, having died this past May. And Bill White — eight times an All-Star at first base, then the National League's president from 1989 to 1994 and the first Black man to head any major league in American sport — completes the slate.4 The Herald, which holds no vote and wants none, will observe only that a ballot wanting twelve hands from sixteen has broken harder hearts than Piniella's twice already, and will report the arithmetic faithfully come December.

THE OPTIONS LEDGER, FOURTH DAY: MILWAUKEE KEEPS THE CATCHER WHO CAUGHT A THOUSAND INNINGS THRICE RUNNING, DETROIT TURNS ITS OLD CLOSER LOOSE STILL SHORT OF FIVE HUNDRED SAVES, AND BALTIMORE PARTS WITH MOUNTCASTLE

The ledger's fourth day began with the least surprising entry of the winter: Milwaukee exercised its $15.5 million option on William Contreras, the World Series' most valuable man, who hit .270 with 18 home runs and 94 runs driven in while becoming the first catcher in the franchise's annals to log a thousand innings behind the plate in three consecutive seasons.5 The intrigue is in what follows, for Contreras now enters his final season before free agency, and the club's custom with men so situated has lately been the trade — Burnes dealt before 2024, Williams before 2025, Peralta before 2026 — though the Adames precedent, held to the last day and converted into a draft pick, shows the other road. The question will shadow the winter meetings.5

In Detroit the arithmetic ran the other way. The Tigers declined their $12 million option on Kenley Jansen, paying the $2 million buyout and sending the 39-year-old to market still short of the 500-save mark his career pursues; the season's surface figures — 22 saves, a 3.20 earned-run average — concealed six blown saves and 23 walks in 45 innings, and the club now enters the winter without an established closer.6 They kept the right-hander Drew Anderson at $10 million, his 3.67 figure across 108 innings having earned him rotation work by season's end, and re-signed the reliever Jacob Waguespack.6 In Baltimore, meanwhile, two long-tenured men reached the open market at once: Ryan Mountcastle's $7.5 million option was declined after an injury-wrecked year of just eight games — a foot fracture, then an oblique strain — his position long since crowded out by the five-year, $155 million signing of Pete Alonso last December; and Heston Kjerstad, the second overall pick of the 2020 draft, cleared waivers, was outrighted, and becomes a minor-league free agent at 27, his great promise still unredeemed. The outfielder Leody Taveras elected free agency besides.7

THE RUMOR DESK: THE NORTH SIDERS ARE SAID TO WANT THE FAIR'S FIRST LOT 'BADLY' — SIX OF CHICAGO'S STARTING ARMS WALK FREE AT ONCE, AND SKUBAL WOULD RESTOCK THE SHELF AT A STROKE

The winter market being one day old, the first great courtship is already whispered. ESPN's Jeff Passan reports that the Cubs "badly want" Tarik Skubal — the man this paper ranked the undisputed first lot of the fair only yesterday — and the arithmetic explains the ardor: six of Chicago's starting pitchers at once — Shota Imanaga, Matthew Boyd, Kevin Gausman, Clay Holmes, David Peterson and Colin Rea — are free agents, leaving the rotation shelf nearly bare behind the league's best offense. ESPN's Jesse Rogers adds that the club will "entertain almost anyone" where starting pitching is concerned, though the two-time Cy Young winner plainly heads the list.8

The price of such ardor is the rub. The trade's reckoning, carried in these columns since the market's eve, holds Skubal a near-lock to pass Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 million standard for a pitching contract, and MLB.com's Mark Feinsand counts six clubs in the running with more expected to join.8 A club whose Most Valuable Player favorite patrols center field and whose winter purse has historically opened widest on the North Side's great occasions would seem a suitor of the first order; whether it opens $325 million wide, the Herald will learn alongside the reader.

This morning's consultation of the schedule ledger — performed daily, whatever the season — turned up a development of the first order: the page is white no longer. The first ink of 2027 has appeared upon it — sixteen spring exhibitions dated Friday, the 19th of February, the Rockies calling on Arizona and the Angels at Milwaukee among them — 108 mornings from this one, with Opening Night itself still 141 mornings off, on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 Exhibitions turn no volume and settle no standings, but a dated page is a promise, and the Herald records it as such. Nearer at hand: the writers begin reading their verdicts Monday next, the rookies first,2 and the qualifying-offer men have a fortnight to answer their tenders. The winter desk, in short, has a fuller docket than many a July morning. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Second of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 142 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 117 · Monday, the Second of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

142 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE LAURELS DESK: RAWLINGS HANDS DOWN ITS SCORE OF GOLDEN GLOVES AND NINE MEN TAKE THEIR FIRST — THE CRIMSON HOSE AND THE DESERT NINE CLAIM THREE APIECE, THE CHAMPIONS GO TWO FOR TWO, AND WALLS SPOILS WITT'S BID FOR A THIRD

The verdict promised in Sunday's columns arrived on schedule: Rawlings handed down the 2026 Gold Gloves last evening, and for the second year running the honors read like a nursery — nine men collected the first of their careers, a near-team's-worth of new silverware.2 The Red Sox and the Diamondbacks split the laurels' lion's share at three apiece. Boston's trio: the third baseman Caleb Durbin, a first-timer who led the league's third basemen with 13 defensive runs saved in his first season in the Hub; the center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, back to back in center and the first man to repeat there in his league since Kevin Kiermaier in 2015 and 2016; and the right fielder Wilyer Abreu, a winner for the third year running on the strength of those 28 defensive runs saved this paper remarked only yesterday — the most of any man in baseball, by the ledger and now by the trophy case too. Arizona's three: the catcher Gabriel Moreno, a two-time winner and only the second catcher ever to pair a Gold Glove with a batting title in the same season, after Joe Mauer; the shortstop Geraldo Perdomo, whose 16 outs above average finally earned the first of his career; and the right fielder Corbin Carroll, somehow a first-timer himself.2

The contests this paper flagged Sunday resolved as follows. Bobby Witt Jr.'s pursuit of a third consecutive shortstop honor fell short, and so did the challenge of Andrés Giménez: the glove went instead to Taylor Walls, who led all shortstops with 21 defensive runs saved and becomes the first Tampa Bay shortstop ever so honored — the club's first winner at any post since Kiermaier in 2019 — on the very day, the reader will savor, that his employers must rule on his contract clause.2 Steven Kwan's first candidacy in center field fell to Rafaela. Dillon Dingler kept his crown behind the plate for Detroit. Elsewhere in the junior circuit: Christian Walker took his fourth at first base and his first in Houston silks; Seattle's Cole Young, in his second season, became the club's first second-base winner since Bret Boone — whose streak began before Young was born; Cody Bellinger of the Yankees won his second, the first having come as a right fielder with the 2019 Dodgers; Tanner Bibee joined Shane Bieber as Cleveland's only pitching winners; and Ezequiel Duran gave Texas its first utility honor. The Toronto men, who tied for the most finalists in the field with five, came away with empty hands.2

In the elder league the sweetest news went north to Milwaukee, where the lately crowned champions went two for two: Brice Turang took his second glove at second base — his 23 defensive runs saved trailed only Abreu in all of baseball, and he remains the only second baseman in the club's annals to win one — and the 22-year-old Jackson Chourio, errorless the season through in left field, took his first, making them the third and fourth Brewers ever to hold the award in multiple or maiden splendor four days after holding the Commissioner's Trophy.3 Matt Olson of Atlanta won his fourth at first base; his new teammate Mauricio Dubón took the utility honor for a third time, no other man having won it even twice; Alex Bregman became the second Cubs third baseman to win one, the first being Ron Santo; Pete Crow-Armstrong repeated in center on a league-best 26 outs above average, garnish for his 40-40 season at the bat; and Nolan McLean of the Mets became the first rookie pitcher ever to win a Gold Glove — the Flushing nine's first glove at any position since Juan Lagares in 2014.2

THE HERALD LOWERS ITS COLORS: JERRY KOOSMAN, LEFT ARM OF THE MIRACLE METS, IS DEAD AT THREE-AND-EIGHTY — HE THREW THE PITCH THAT ENDED 1969 AND LEAPT INTO GROTE'S ARMS, AND NEW YORK NEVER FORGOT THE SIGHT

Jerry Koosman, perhaps the finest left-handed pitcher ever to wear a Mets uniform, died Sunday at the age of 83.4 For 12 seasons in New York, from 1967 through 1978, he was the other half of the great tandem with Tom Seaver, and the franchise's ledger still carries his name at the top of every left-handed column: 140 wins, 346 starts, 108 complete games, 26 shutouts, 1,799 strikeouts, a 3.09 earned-run average. As a rookie in 1968 he won 19 games with a 2.08 figure and finished second for the league's Rookie of the Year honors only to Johnny Bench — no disgrace in any era.4

It was October of 1969 that fixed him in the city's memory forever. With the Miracle Mets down a game to the Orioles, Koosman played the stopper in Game 2, carrying a no-hitter into the seventh inning of a 2-1 victory; three games later he went the distance in the Game 5 clincher at Shea Stadium and, as the last out settled into history, leapt into the arms of his catcher Jerry Grote — an image the game has never filed away. He added a Championship Series win over the Reds and a World's Series win besides in 1973, a 21-win season in 1976, and the hard-luck badge of a 20-loss season in 1977 carried with a 3.49 earned-run average. The Army had found him before the Mets did: he was signed for $1,600 in 1964 on the recommendation of a Fort Bliss batterymate whose father ushered at Shea Stadium — the cheapest great signing in the franchise's books. Traded to Minnesota after 1978 in the deal that brought back Jesse Orosco, he shares with that man a symmetry no other pair can claim: the two left-handers who stood on the mound for the final out of each of the Mets' two world championships. Over 19 seasons with the Mets, Twins, White Sox and Phillies he won 222 games, struck out 2,556 men, and pitched his last at 42. The club retired his No. 36 in August of 2021, making him then only the third player in its history so honored. "He was a warrior," his old teammate Ron Swoboda once said. "He played the whole game all the time."4 The Herald lowers its colors for the warrior of Shea: may every left arm that follows him in Flushing be measured against his, and may none mind falling short.

THE FAR PACIFIC DESK: SATO, TRIPLE CROWN MAN OF THE CENTRAL LEAGUE, IS POSTED AND MAY TREAT WITH ALL THIRTY CLUBS FROM THIS VERY DAY — ITOH OF THE FIGHTERS FOLLOWS HIM ACROSS, AND THE EASTERN CONTINGENT GROWS TO THREE

The grandest bat of the winter's eastern fleet has weighed anchor. Teruaki Sato, the Hanshin Tigers' slugging third baseman, was made available through the posting process Sunday, and negotiations with all 30 clubs are permitted to begin this very Monday.5 The credentials want little embroidery: the left-handed hitter took the Central League's Triple Crown this season at .306 with 39 home runs and 106 runs driven in, atop the league's Most Valuable Player award he carried home in 2025. He will play next season at 28, old enough that no restriction binds the terms he may command, with Hanshin to collect a release fee scaled to the contract he signs and a 45-day window in which to sign it. The scouts' cavils are two: a 27 percent strikeout rate that invites comparison to Munetaka Murakami — who struck out more and still hit 35 home runs as a White Sox rookie this season — and a question of where he fields, with 262 games of outfield work on his Japanese ledger if third base will not serve. The insider Jon Heyman has linked the Mets, Yankees, Dodgers and Phillies to the man; in a market thin on power hitting, the queue seems likely to lengthen.5

Behind him came an arm. The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters on Sunday officially posted the right-hander Hiromi Itoh, 29, whose six seasons read 2.92 by earned-run average across a thousand innings, and whose 2025 campaign — a 2.52 figure with 195 strikeouts — won him the Sawamura Award, Japan's answer to the Cy Young.6 This season he gave 172 2/3 innings at 3.18 while walking fewer than five men in a hundred. He joins Sato and the little Seibu right-hander Kaima Taira, whose coming passage this paper logged Saturday, in a contingent from the far shore now three strong — with more sails reported on the horizon.6

THE BAZAAR DESK: THE GATES SWING OPEN AT FIVE O'CLOCK THIS AFTERNOON — SAN DIEGO KEEPS ITS THREE LEFT HANDS AND TURNS TWO RIGHT ONES LOOSE, BOSTON RETAINS ITS SETUP MAN, AND THE DECEMBER CLOCK HURRIES EVERY BIDDER

At 5 o'clock Eastern this afternoon the exclusive courtships end and the winter market opens to all comers, precisely as this paper's ledger has been promising all week. The catalogue is set: Tarik Skubal stands the undisputed first lot, a near-lock by the trade's reckoning to pass Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 million standard for a pitching contract; Michael King, whose opt-out this paper recorded Friday, ranks second; and third comes Freddy Peralta, whose season turned from a 4.99 earned-run average in a Mets uniform to a 3.25 in Tampa Bay colors after a midsummer trade, then to the Championship Series' most-valuable honors in October.7 Sato, newly posted, ranks fourth, and over the whole fair hangs the first of December, when the collective agreement expires — a deadline that five years ago drove Corey Seager, Marcus Semien, Max Scherzer and three other nine-figure men to sign before the Thanksgiving leftovers were finished. The December clock, in short, may make this a sprinting market rather than a strolling one.7

The last of the option rulings came in under the wire. San Diego will keep all three of its left-handed relievers: Yuki Matsui opted into his $6.5 million season on the heels of a 1.83 earned-run average across 54 outings, joining Wandy Peralta — whose own opt-in this ledger recorded Sunday — and Kyle Hart, whose club option was exercised; the Friars meanwhile declined their mutual options on the right-handers Lucas Giolito and Griffin Canning, and Miguel Andújar declined his own, all three joining the market. The club has until 2 o'clock Pacific today to decide a qualifying offer for the setup man Adrian Morejon, the best-performing reliever of the free-agent class by the past three seasons' ledger.8 And in Boston the Red Sox exercised their $8.25 million option on Garrett Whitlock, whose 1.72 earned-run average and 0.90 WHIP across 54 appearances made him the sturdiest bridge to the ninth inning in the league — a Rule 5 plucking from the Yankees, the reader may enjoy recalling, that has repaid Boston for six years running.9

THE APPOINTMENTS DESK: FLORES TAKES HIS CHAIR AT DAIKIN PARK THIS VERY DAY AND THE MANAGER HUNT OPENS AT ONCE — AUSMUS, THRICE A GOLDEN GLOVER IN HOUSTON SILKS HIMSELF, STANDS IN THE RUNNING

Randy Flores, whose hiring this paper reported Saturday, is introduced to the press this day at Daikin Park, and the Houston club means to waste no time on the vacancy beneath him: with the general managers convening at Las Vegas next week, the hunt for a manager to succeed Joe Espada is already under way.10 The name at the head of the speculation is a familiar one in those parts. Brad Ausmus — who caught more games than any man in the franchise's history across ten seasons, won three Gold Gloves in Houston silks, and handled the celebrated staffs of 2004 and 2005 — was in the offices at Daikin Park on Thursday, by the word of multiple sources, interviewing for the general manager's post by one account, with a chance the club now gives him a look for the manager's chair instead. The credentials cut both ways: three seasons lately as the Yankees' bench coach and close ties to the club adviser Jeff Bagwell on the one hand; a 386-422 managerial record with the Tigers and Angels on the other. He interviewed for this same chair in 2020, when it went to Dusty Baker.10

The new man's own history may widen the field. Flores spent five of his pitching years and ten of his office years in St. Louis, and two of his old teammates there — Albert Pujols and Yadier Molina — have each declared the ambition to manage in the big leagues. Molina has piloted Puerto Rico in two World Baseball Classics, won with his clubs in the Venezuelan winter league, and lately joined the Cardinals as a special assistant; Pujols managed the Dominican side in this year's Classic and led Escogido to both the Dominican league and Caribbean Series titles a winter ago. Whether the old battery of Cardinal loyalties produces Houston's next skipper, the Herald will report as the interviews proceed.10

The paper goes to press this Monday with the bazaar's gates still barred; by suppertime they stand open, and every free man in the game may talk terms with any of thirty clubs. The schedule ledger has been consulted all the same, as it is every morning, and stands white for 142 mornings more, until Opening Night on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027.1 But let no reader mistake a white schedule for a quiet one: the gloves came down last night, the market opens this afternoon, and the general managers pack for Las Vegas next week with the December labor clock audible in every valise.10 The Herald's winter desk is fully staffed and entirely unbothered — there is a kind of box score in a contract ledger too, if you squint. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the First of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 143 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 116 · Sunday, the First of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

143 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE RETENTIONS DESK: TAMPA BAY KEEPS ITS ACE AT A WAGE OF TWENTY MILLIONS, A SUM NEVER BEFORE PAID ON THE BAYFRONT — AND THE QUESTION OF A TRADE ARRIVES IN THE SAME ENVELOPE

The first great ruling of the options ledger this paper has kept all week came down Saturday night, and it kept an ace in harness. The Rays exercised their $20 million club option on the right-hander Drew Rasmussen — the decision this ledger noted Friday as still pending — and thereby committed to the largest single-season salary in the franchise's history, whose previous high-water mark was the $15 million paid Charlie Morton in 2019.3 The figure was earned the hard way: the option, written into his January 2025 extension at $8 million, carried escalators the pitcher maxed out entirely with the finest season of his career — 16 wins against 5 defeats, a 2.67 earned-run average and 174 strikeouts across 172 innings and 30 starts, the American League's best WHIP at 0.91 — followed by an October in which he opened with three gems and closed by taking the ball in the fifth game of the World's Series on three days' rest, the first such assignment of his life, and allowing one run on two hits over four innings of a losing cause. Since 2022 his 2.74 earned-run average stands fourth among all pitchers with 500 innings, behind only Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Chris Sale.3

The celebration is tempered by arithmetic. A club that has never paid any man $20 million must now decide whether to pay this one or trade him, and the pitcher knows it — asked after the fifth game whether he hoped to remain, he answered "I hope so," then added, "There's a business element to this, and I understand that." His manager Kevin Cash was less equivocal: "He's a stud. That guy is a stud." With Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez both departed to the open market, the St. Petersburg club's winter turns on what it does with the arm it just retained.3

THE OPTIONS LEDGER, THIRD DAY: SAN DIEGO TURNS PIVETTA LOOSE AND KEEPS A LEFT-HANDER, BALTIMORE PARTS WITH ROBERT, CINCINNATI'S CLOSER WALKS AWAY FROM TEN MILLIONS OF HIS OWN ACCORD, AND THREE RANGERS TAKE THEIR LEAVE

Elsewhere the ledger ran heavy with departures. The Padres declined their $14 million option on the right-hander Nick Pivetta, by the word of a source, though the club has not confirmed it and professes interest in signing him back at a friendlier figure.4 The elbow wrote this entry: Pivetta, entering his age-34 season, made only eight starts in 2026 around a flexor strain that cost him nearly five months, and the long stay on the infirmary list triggered a clause converting what had been his own option into the club's. He pitched well on his return — a 1.45 earned-run average over his final four starts, then two honest October outings — but with Michael King already opted out and Casey Mize, Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler all free besides, the San Diego rotation is suddenly mostly vacancies. The left-handed reliever Wandy Peralta, for his part, exercised his $4.45 million option to stay.4 In Baltimore the Birds declined their $20 million figure on the outfielder Luis Robert Jr., as this ledger foresaw they might — the 29-year-old played all of three games in their colors after an August waiver claim before a hamstring ended his season, and he departs with a $2 million buyout, the club's door pointedly left ajar for a cheaper reunion. Only the first baseman Ryan Mountcastle's $7.5 million clause remains on the Baltimore docket.5

The day's genuine surprise came from Cincinnati, where the closer Emilio Pagán declined his $10 million player option and walked into the market at 35.6 The Queen City nine had watched him save 25 games this season at a 3.38 earned-run average — and, after returning from a spring hamstring strain on July 1, convert every one of his 19 chances at a 1.88 figure over his final 30 appearances — and must now hunt a ninth-inning man in a winter when Raisel Iglesias, David Bednar and Adrian Morejon are likewise at large. The third baseman Eugenio Suárez, whose second tour in Cincinnati yielded 26 home runs but a .212 average, and the reliever Pierce Johnson had their mutual options declined the same afternoon.6 And in Texas, the designated hitter Joc Pederson, the catcher Kyle Higashioka and the right-hander Jakob Junis all declined their mutual options with the Lone Star nine.7 The whole settling of accounts must finish within five days of the Series' end, and come Monday at 5 o'clock Eastern the market opens to all comers.69

THE LAURELS DESK: A SCORE OF GOLDEN GLOVES IS HANDED DOWN THIS VERY EVENING — TURANG OF THE CHAMPIONS STANDS AMONG THE FINALISTS, WITT PURSUES A THIRD IN SUCCESSION, AND KWAN SEEKS A FIFTH FROM A NEW PASTURE

The fielding season receives its verdict tonight: the Rawlings Gold Glove winners are unveiled this evening at 8:30 Eastern, with three finalists standing at every position in each league.8 The electorate is the game's own bench — each club's manager and up to six coaches, barred from voting for their own men, supply three-quarters of the reckoning, with the Society for American Baseball Research's defensive index the remaining quarter. The Blue Jays and Cubs lead the field with five finalists apiece.8 Milwaukee's interest is direct: Brice Turang, lately seen turning the final out of the World's Series, is a finalist at second base. Tampa Bay's shortstop Taylor Walls — whose contract clause, it happens, still awaits the club's ruling — is a finalist for the second straight year.8

The contests worth watching: Bobby Witt Jr. of the Royals pursues a third consecutive honor at shortstop, where Andrés Giménez — thrice a winner at second base — now challenges from his new post; Steven Kwan of the Guardians, four years running the winner in left field, stands for the first time as a center-field finalist, having manned the middle pasture more often than the corner this season; Wilyer Abreu of the Red Sox arrives with 28 defensive runs saved, the most of any man in baseball by a wide margin; and Dillon Dingler of the Tigers defends his crown behind the plate. The Herald, by its standing rule, hands out nothing before the ballot does — the names of the anointed in tomorrow's columns.8

THE BAZAAR DESK: THE WINTER MARKET OPENS ITS STALLS ON THE MORROW — SKUBAL THE PRIZE OF THE FAIR, THE QUALIFYING OFFER SET AT THREE-AND-TWENTY MILLIONS AND CHANGE, AND THE LABOR CLOCK TICKING TOWARD DECEMBER

With the options ledger closing, the shape of the winter fair is plain, and the grandest stall belongs to Tarik Skubal. The left-hander, twice the American League's Cy Young man,2 split his season between Detroit and Los Angeles and arrives at the market bearing a ledger of 50 wins against 20 defeats and a 2.47 earned-run average across 103 starts since 2023.9 The sums under discussion strain the type: the largest pitching contract on record is Yoshinobu Yamamoto's twelve years and $325 million, and the highest annual wage the $43.33 million shared by Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander — marks the trade expects Skubal to pass and to press, respectively, with the Mets, Dodgers, Tigers, Blue Jays and Cubs all named among the likely bidders.9

The almanac fills in around him. The qualifying offer is fixed this year at $23.15 million, and the week ahead brings the usual parlor game of who receives one — Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki all but certainly, each all but certain to decline. The general managers convene at Las Vegas from November 9 through 11, where the winter's first trade winds customarily begin to blow. And over the whole bazaar hangs the first of December, when the collective agreement between the clubs and the players expires.9 The Herald will watch that negotiation with its customary interest — and when the pleading of empty purses begins, as it reliably does, this paper will be found consulting the ledger rather than the handkerchief.

THE FOOTLIGHTS DESK: THE SUDS MEN PLAY ROCKEFELLER CENTER — YELICH, TURANG AND MURPHY CROSS WITS WITH A DRUNKEN UNCLE ON THE SATURDAY BROADCAST, TWO-AND-FORTY YEARS AFTER UECKER HELD THE SAME STAGE

The champions' victory tour reached television's oldest vaudeville house Saturday night, when Christian Yelich, Brice Turang and the manager Pat Murphy appeared together on Saturday Night Live's Weekend Update segment, charged with convincing the returning character Drunk Uncle — the comedian Bobby Moynihan, back at the Update desk — that a team named for beermaking had truly won the World's Series.10 The sketch found time for an old wound: "Hey, wait a minute," Moynihan said, eyeing the Milwaukee captain. "You're Pete Davidson, right?" — a jab at a resemblance that has trailed Yelich since his Miami days.10

The Herald notes the echo in the rafters. The club's last man on that stage was Bob Uecker himself, who hosted the second episode of the program's tenth season on October 13 of 1984, in the full flower of his beer-advertisement and Tonight Show celebrity.10 Forty-two years later, the franchise he voiced for half a century sent three world's champions up the same elevators — one more small ceremony, after Friday's parade and the coin in the clubhouse man's pocket, in an autumn that keeps finding ways to toast the old announcer.

The clocks fell back overnight, and so the game's first Sunday of winter arrives an hour longer than the Saturday before it — a cruel arithmetic, the reader will note, since the extra hour contains precisely as much baseball as the other twenty-four. The schedule ledger has been consulted this morning all the same, and stands white for 143 mornings more, until Opening Night on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027.1 But the paper is not without appointments: the Gold Gloves are handed down this very evening,8 the market throws open its gates Monday at 5 o'clock,6 and the first hardware of awards season will keep these columns warm straight through to the truck that leaves for the training camps. An hour gained and 143 to wait — the Herald suggests spending the found one on the archive. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 115 · Saturday, the Thirty-First of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

144 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE PROCESSION DESK: THREE-QUARTERS OF A MILLION TURN OUT FOR THE CHAMPIONS — THE POLICE CALL IT PERHAPS THE LARGEST GATHERING IN WISCONSIN'S HISTORY, YOUNT RIDES IN ON UECKER'S HARLEY, AND FRELICK PLEDGES A HUNDRED THOUSAND BEERS

The procession this paper trailed yesterday morning came off grander than even Milwaukee dared forecast. By the constabulary's count more than 750,000 souls turned out for the parade and the rally that followed — a figure the police say may stand, their preliminary arithmetic suggests, as the largest crowd for a single day's event in the state's history.2 Fans staked their places along Wisconsin Avenue before dawn; by 8 o'clock thousands had already filled the lakefront grounds at Henry Maier Festival Park, where the 23,000-seat amphitheater held the rally and every stage on the 75 acres carried it by screen. The only prior parade in the club's annals, in 1982, honored a team that had lost the seventh game of the World's Series in St. Louis. This one, 44 years later, honored winners.

The rostrum ran long and merry. Robin Yount arrived astride Bob Uecker's Harley-Davidson, precisely as he did at the rally of 1982, and Ted Simmons spoke for the men of that older club; Rollie Fingers praised the bullpen and the scoreless-innings man Aaron Ashby by name. The Series' most valuable player William Contreras thanked the multitude in English; Brice Turang confessed what the final out had done to his nerves; the captain Christian Yelich called the day worth its long wait; and the hitting coach Daniel Vogelbach sang karaoke. The manager Pat Murphy rode the route at the parade's rear in a lawn chair with his children and quoted Bruce Springsteen from the stage, the owner Mark Attanasio pronounced the state's 6 million residents "one family" for the day, and the president of baseball operations Matt Arnold addressed the crowd with a beer in hand — a detail the crowd took as a credential. As for Sal Frelick, whose leap into the Lambeau stands this paper reported yesterday, he surveyed the sea of humanity and vowed to drink 100,000 beers in its honor — a program this desk neither endorses nor entirely doubts.2

THE OPTIONS LEDGER, SECOND DAY: TAMPA BAY TURNS LOOSE THE ARM THAT WON FIFTEEN AND THE GLOVE THAT ROAMED CENTER — WHILE BALTIMORE PAYS EFLIN TWO MILLIONS TO MEND HIS ELBOW ON THE OPEN MARKET

The settling of accounts that opened Thursday, as this paper's ledger recorded yesterday, ran through its second day without pause. The Gulf Coast club declined its mutual options on the pitcher Nick Martinez and the center fielder Cedric Mullins on Friday, loosing both to the market.3 Martinez, 36, gave Tampa Bay everything $9 million could reasonably buy — 15 wins against 6 defeats, a 3.10 earned-run average across 180 innings and 31 starts, and 16 October innings of five-run ball atop it — but the club chose the $4 million buyout over a $20 million encore, and the pitcher is reported to have declined his own half of the bargain in any case. Mullins required less deliberation: the one-time Oriole batted .205 with 15 home runs and 21 stolen bases in 137 games, and the half-million-dollar buyout was always the likelier end of his $10 million clause. The Tampa men must still rule on Drew Rasmussen's $20 million figure and a smaller one on the shortstop Taylor Walls before Monday.3

In Baltimore the ledger closed on Zach Eflin the way all parties expected: the Baltimores declined his $25 million mutual option and will pay the 32-year-old right-hander a $2 million buyout to seek his fortune on a mending elbow.4 Eflin's season amounted to one start — he left his debut on March 31 with elbow trouble and underwent the Tommy John operation on April 8 — yet he kept close to the club through his rehabilitation and professes a wish to return, so a reunion is not foreclosed. He joins a general exodus from the Baltimore rotation, Trevor Rogers, Chris Bassitt, Keegan Akin and Andrew Kittredge all likewise free, though the bullpen at least holds firm: Ryan Helsley chose the warm hearth on Thursday, as this paper set down yesterday, and the club has decisions yet to make on its outfielder Luis Robert Jr. and first baseman Ryan Mountcastle.4

THE APPOINTMENTS DESK: HOUSTON GOES TO THE CARDINALS' SCHOOLHOUSE FOR ITS NEW GENERAL MANAGER — FLORES, A LEFT-HANDER OF THREE-HUNDRED-AND-FIFTY GAMES IN HIS PITCHING DAYS, MUST FIRST FIND THE CLUB A MANAGER

The Houston nine filled their long-vacant front chair Friday night, naming Randy Flores general manager — the fourth such hire of the owner Jim Crane's tenure, and the end of a search that began when the club parted with Dana Brown better than two months ago.5 Flores, 51, comes from ten seasons in the St. Louis office, where he arrived in 2015 as director of scouting and served as an assistant general manager from 2019 onward. His is a varied résumé even by the modern front office's standards: a left-handed reliever in 350 major-league games for the Cardinals, Rockies, Rangers and Twins; a pitching coach at Southern California; a television analyst; the founder of a sports-video concern. "Randy has had a huge impact on the Cardinals over the last 10 seasons," said Crane, praising his new man's eye for talent.5

The work will not wait for the introductions, which come Monday at Daikin Park. The Astros won the American League West at 81-81 — an eighth divisional flag in ten seasons, and surely the least ornamented of the lot — and then declined to renew the manager Joe Espada after three seasons. Flores' first labor is therefore to find the club a manager, with a bench coach and sundry staff positions to fill behind him.5

THE FAR PACIFIC DESK: THE LOWEST EARNED-RUN FIGURE IN JAPAN ASKS FOR PASSAGE — SEIBU WILL POST THE RIGHT-HANDER TAIRA AND HIS 1.36, AND ALL THIRTY CLUBS GET FIVE-AND-FORTY DAYS TO BID

The winter market gains an arm from across the Pacific. The Saitama Seibu Lions announced they will approve the posting of the right-hander Kaima Taira, who led all of Nippon Professional Baseball in earned-run average this season — a 1.36 figure with a 0.96 WHIP across 23 games in his return to the rotation, after years of distinguished relief work that included a 1.71 average and 31 saves in 2025. Across eight NPB seasons the man's ledger reads 1.78.6 He turns 27 on November 15; once the posting is official, all 30 clubs will have a 45-day window to treat with him, with no restriction on the terms since he is past 25, and Seibu collecting a release fee scaled to whatever deal he strikes.

The scouts' reports read warmly: a fastball run up to the mid-to-upper 90s from a frame of just 5-foot-8, with a cutter, sweeper, changeup and splitter behind it, and a studious turn of mind toward the analytics besides.6 The skeptic's note concerns the frame — only Marcus Stroman, since Fred Norman in 1979, has pitched 100 innings in a season at that height or shorter, and some clubs will fancy Taira a reliever for exactly that reason, though his preference for starting may steer where he signs. He joins Teruaki Sato, the Hanshin Tigers slugger who took the Central League's Triple Crown, among the first NPB men seeking passage to these shores this winter.6

THE COMMERCE DESK: THE WINTER'S SECOND SWAP IS STRUCK FOR PLAIN COIN — DETROIT BUYS THE FOUR-TIMES-CLAIMED CHENG FROM BOSTON, AND THE WAIVER WIRE'S GREAT WANDERER GETS A PERCH

The winter's second trade followed its first by a single day, and was more modest still. Detroit on Friday acquired the infielder Tsung-Che Cheng from the Fenway men for cash considerations — the Bengals' first move of the offseason.7 Cheng, 25, a left-handed-hitting shortstop and second baseman from Taiwan who stands 5-foot-8, knows the waiver wire as a commuter knows his streetcar: cast off by Pittsburgh last offseason after five years in that system, he was claimed by the Rays, the Mets, the Nationals and the Red Sox inside a single month. Boston needed the roster room for men returning from the long infirmary list; Detroit paid cash rather than wait and bid against the wire.

The season past gave the little infielder his first major-league hit, on June 26 in his Boston debut, and a .256 average over 14 games in the big club's employ, with a .241/.345/.390 line and 8 home runs across 94 games at Worcester beneath it. In Detroit he finds a familiar face: the infielder Hao-Yu Lee, his countryman and teammate on the Chinese Taipei side at the World Baseball Classic, where Cheng reached base eight times in four games and stole four bags. The Bengals' own arithmetic now presses — 36 men on the roster of 40, with eight more to be accommodated off the 60-day infirmary list by Monday — so the wanderer's perch, it must be said, is not yet a guaranteed one.7

All Hallows' Eve, and for once the calendar's costume holiday finds the game with nothing left to disguise. The schedule page stands white this morning, as it will for 144 mornings more, until Opening Night restores the genuine article on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027.1 The Herald's lamps stay lit regardless: the options ledger runs through Monday,3 the awards season draws near, and the first arms from Japan are already asking for harbor. Let the neighborhood's small goblins have their evening — this desk has watched a Milwaukee club that spent fifty-seven seasons dressed as a contender finally take the mask off, and no store-bought fright will top it. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Thirtieth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 145 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 114 · Friday, the Thirtieth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

145 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE MARKET DESK: THE LAST OUT BARELY RECORDED AND THE WINTER BAZAAR THROWS OPEN ITS DOORS — KING DECLINES HIS OPTION AND WALKS OUT OF SAN DIEGO AS THE PRIZE ARM OF THE CLASS, AT TWO-AND-THIRTY

The World's Series ended Wednesday night; by Thursday the game had changed its business from pennants to purses. Michael King has declined the player option on his contract with the Padres, by the word of sources given to MLB.com, and steps onto the market as one of the foremost arms available entering his age-32 season. The right-hander earned the billing honestly in 2026 — a 3.21 earned-run average across 32 starts, worth a career-best 4.3 wins by the ledger's accounting — and salted his October with two starts of one run across 12 innings and 14 strikeouts, plus a two-inning save besides in the third game of the Division Series against the eventual champions.2 He leaves two years of a three-year, $75 million engagement on the table and collects a $5 million buyout for his trouble; San Diego holds the exclusive right to treat with him until Monday, and the two parties are reported still interested in a reunion. "San Diego has been incredible for me," the pitcher said upon the Friars' autumn exit. "I feel like I have a second home on the West Coast. It's been awesome. And I hope to continue it."2

Every club now does its winter sums, and none more gravely than the North Siders of Chicago, who watched the division rival they could not catch parade off with the whole pot. The Cubs could lose every one of the five men who finished the season in their rotation: Shota Imanaga, Kevin Gausman and David Peterson became free agents Thursday, Matthew Boyd and Clay Holmes are expected to join them by way of their option clauses, and Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki head the list of departing bats.3 The president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer, asked at his season's-end accounting why the gap to Milwaukee keeps widening, pointed at the champions' mound: "Their pitching has been exceptionally good. I think that's the area that we have to double down and really focus on."3

THE FIDELITY DESK: TWO MEN WEIGH THE OPEN ROAD AGAINST THE WARM HEARTH AND CHOOSE THE HEARTH — BICHETTE TAKES HIS TWO-AND-FORTY MILLIONS IN FLUSHING, HELSLEY HIS FOURTEEN IN BALTIMORE

Not every man with a door to the market walked through it. Bo Bichette has opted into the second season of his three-year, $126 million engagement, a source advises, and will reprise his role as the Metropolitans' third baseman at $42 million for 2027 — with the same escape clause waiting for him again next autumn. The first year in Queens was an uneven one: booed while going 1-for-14 across his first three home games, carrying an OPS below .600 as late as the 10th of June, then batting .285/.337/.442 the rest of the way — recovery enough for comfort, if not for the kind of winter that beats $84 million guaranteed. At 28 he has also grown into the role of tutor to the young men A.J. Ewing and Carson Benge, and by season's end professed himself considerably happier in the uniform than he began.4

In Baltimore, Ryan Helsley reached the same conclusion by a harder road. The right-hander is opting into his $14 million player option for 2027, a source confirms, after an injury-plagued season — a 4.11 earned-run average and eight saves in only 17 games, two stays in the infirmary for his elbow, and not a single appearance after the 27th of June, though the club expects him whole for the spring. The Birds' bullpen thus enters the winter holding both Helsley and the lately mended Félix Bautista, and the question of which man closes is now Baltimore's pleasant arithmetic to perform.5

THE OPTIONS LEDGER: ATLANTA SPENDS FOUR-AND-TWENTY MILLIONS TO KEEP ACUÑA AND ALBIES IN HARNESS, SEATTLE RETAINS ITS CLOSER, AND KANSAS CITY TURNS ITS OWN LOOSE

The day's heaviest traffic ran through the option clauses, where clubs across both leagues settled accounts. Atlanta exercised Ronald Acuña Jr.'s $17 million option and Ozzie Albies' $7 million one, keeping the old cornerstones side by side at least one season more. Acuña's year was the now-familiar mixture of brilliance and the trainer's table — .255 with 20 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a .796 OPS in 107 games, a third of the schedule lost to two separate hamstring strains, with a .997 OPS over his final 26 games to argue the talent remains. A further $17 million option for 2028 waits in his contract; Albies may test the market after 2027.6

In Seattle the Mariners exercised Andrés Muñoz's $9 million option despite the most trying season of his career — a 4.24 earned-run average and 10 blown saves, tying the most in the majors — while declining Bryce Miller's $6.075 million figure, though the right-hander remains under the club's control through arbitration to 2029. Victor Robles was let go to free agency, joining Randy Arozarena, J.P. Crawford, Hoby Milner and Taylor Ward among the Puget Sound men now free to sign anywhere beginning Monday afternoon.7 And in Kansas City the Royals declined their $13 million option on the closer Carlos Estévez — who led all baseball with 42 saves in 2025 and now takes a $2 million buyout to the open market — while exercising a $2.5 million option on the mending right-hander Tony Gonsolin, a 16-game winner for the 2022 Dodgers whom they will try in rotation or relief come spring.8

THE COMMERCE DESK: THE WINTER'S FIRST SWAP IS STRUCK BEFORE THE CHAMPAGNE IS MOPPED — THE WHITE ELEPHANTS FETCH THE UTILITY MAN EATON FROM THE HUB NINE FOR AN ARM OF EIGHTEEN SUMMERS

It wanted less than 24 hours after the final out for the first trade of the offseason to be struck. The Athletics on Thursday acquired the outfielder Nate Eaton from the Red Sox in exchange for the minor-league right-hander Jareth Rayo. Eaton, 29, caught in the crush of Boston's 40-man roster, batted a thin .160 in 24 games this season but carries a defender's résumé — all three outfield posts and third base besides — and gives the Athletics seasoned depth for the upper rungs of their system. Rayo, 18, signed out of Nicaragua in the 2024-25 international period, posted a 5.50 earned-run average with 36 strikeouts against 20 walks across 36 innings of the Dominican Summer League.9

The footnote is the front office. The swap is the first official act of Taylor Smith, the Athletics' newly installed president of baseball operations — and it was struck with the very Boston office he served under Craig Breslow from 2024 through this past season. The winter's dealings have begun with a man trading against his own former desk.9

THE PROCESSION DESK: MILWAUKEE SHUTS ITS SCHOOLHOUSES AND LINES WISCONSIN AVENUE THIS MORNING — THE CHAMPIONS SPENT THEIR EVE AT LAMBEAU FIELD, AND THE RELICS ARE ALREADY BOUND FOR COOPERSTOWN

The Parade of Champions, whose particulars this paper set down yesterday, steps off this very morning: 10 o'clock Central time, from North 4th Street and West Wisconsin Avenue, with the rally and fan festival to follow at Henry Maier Festival Park, all of it free to whoever arrives first. The city has cleared the way in the most literal sense — Milwaukee Public Schools closed every school and district office for the day, "due to operations and safety impacts from the Brewers parade and celebration," the official notice crowned with the words "Congrats World Champs."10

The champions rehearsed their celebrating Thursday night in Green Bay, where a cadre of Brewers — the veteran pitcher Brandon Woodruff striding at the front with the Commissioner's Trophy held high — crashed the Packers' game against the Panthers at Lambeau Field to a roar from the house. Sal Frelick, whose game-squaring home run turned the second game of the Series, could not resist the local sacrament: a picture-perfect Lambeau Leap into the first row beyond the end zone.11 And the museum men have already claimed their share of the October just closed. Bound for the Hall of Fame at Cooperstown: the chest protector and shin guards of the Series' most valuable player William Contreras, the manager Pat Murphy's postseason hooded sweatshirt, the unmistakable spectacles of the scoreless-innings man Aaron Ashby, and Frelick's batting gloves from that second game.12

A strange quiet this morning: for the first time since March, no contest stands behind this paper and none ahead of it. The schedule ledger has been consulted all the same, as it is every morning, and the page is white — 145 mornings of it, until Opening Night restores the game on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027, with the full slate following a day later.1 The Herald does not fold its tent for the cold months. The market opened within hours of the last out, as the columns above attest; the awards season and the winter's dealings lie ahead; and this paper will keep its daily watch over all of it, from the first opt-out to the last truck bound for the training camps. Today, though, belongs to Milwaukee, where the schoolhouses stand empty and Wisconsin Avenue fills. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
